pages.body:
Section 5 and Appendix C hold every part of [[bert]] fixed except one, then re-run the experiment to see what that one part was worth. The programme is here because BERT's headline results change several things at once relative to prior work — a bidirectional objective, a second sentence-level objective, more data, a bigger model — and a table of wins cannot say which of those changes earned them.

### The thing being held fixed

Each ablation is its own pre-training run from scratch. The [[pre-training-data|pre-training corpus]], the fine-tuning scheme and the hyperparameters are pinned to BERT_BASE's values, and only the named facet moves. That control is what licenses the paper to charge a particular drop in score to a particular removal.

Five facets are varied across the two locations. [[effect-of-pre-training-tasks]] takes away [[next-sentence-prediction]], then takes away bidirectionality on top of that ([[table-5]]). [[effect-of-model-size]] walks a ladder of six separately pre-trained configurations, from three layers up to twenty-four ([[table-6]]). [[feature-based-approach-with-bert]] freezes BERT and reads features off it instead of fine-tuning ([[table-7]]). Appendix C adds [[effect-of-number-of-training-steps]] ([[fig-5]]) and [[masking-procedure-ablation]] ([[table-8]]).

### What the design costs

Pinning the recipe has a price. The left-to-right variant, [[ltr-no-nsp-ablation]], is described as directly comparable to [[openai-gpt]], but it is trained on BERT's larger corpus with BERT's [[input-representation]] and BERT's fine-tuning scheme. So it isolates bidirectionality more cleanly than a comparison against published GPT numbers would, while no longer being a measurement of GPT.

The other price is sample size. A row in these tables is one pre-training run at roughly a million steps, so there is one run per setting and no repeated pre-training seeds anywhere. The error bars that do exist come from fine-tuning restarts only: Tables 6 and 7 average five random restarts, Table 5 does not say.

### How strong the evidence is

These are [[dev-set-model-selection|Dev set]] numbers on subsets of tasks — four GLUE tasks for the size ladder, MNLI and NER for the masking mixture. They are evidence about relative importance, not results to compare against other systems.

What carries weight is direction rather than magnitude. Perplexity falls at every rung of the size ladder and accuracy rises at every rung; the left-to-right model loses on every task in Table 5. The individual gaps are often a point or two on small Dev sets — MRPC has 3,600 training examples — so any single cell is soft. And where the paper explains the size result, it marks the explanation as a hypothesis: see [[few-random-parameters-hypothesis]].

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

pages.body:
BERT is a language representation model that is pre-trained once on [[unlabeled-text]], then fine-tuned separately for each task with one new output layer added on top. It is in the paper as an answer to a specific complaint: the pre-training objectives in use at the time read text in one direction only, which the authors argue restricts which architectures can be pre-trained at all, and hurts transfer most on [[token-level-tasks|token-level tasks]] ([[unidirectionality-constraint]]).

That complaint has a named target. [[openai-gpt]] pre-trains a Transformer language model left to right, then fine-tunes every parameter on the labeled task. BERT is an instance of the same [[fine-tuning-approach|fine-tuning strategy]], not a rival to it.

The paper says it kept the two as close as it could. [[bert-base-and-bert-large|BERT_BASE]] has 12 layers, [[hidden-size-h|hidden size]] 768 and 12 attention heads, 110M parameters in total, chosen to equal GPT's size. What is left to differ is direction. [[fig-3]] states that as arrows, with [[elmo]] as a third case whose two one-way stacks meet only at the very top.

### What the model actually does

Pre-training runs [[bert-model-architecture|a multi-layer Transformer encoder]] in which every token attends to every other token at every layer ([[deep-bidirectionality]]). An ordinary language-model loss cannot be trained that way, because a token that sees context on both sides can reach its own prediction through the stack.

The substitute is [[masked-language-model|the masked LM]]: hide a random 15% of the token positions and predict the originals from what is left. In a 512-token sequence that is about 77 predictions per example. A second objective, [[next-sentence-prediction]], asks whether the second packed span really followed the first, and the two losses are summed.

Both objectives run over one input format ([[input-representation]]): a single token sequence holding either one text or two, where each token's vector is the elementwise sum of a token, a segment and a position embedding ([[fig-2]]).

[[fine-tuning-bert|Fine-tuning]] then changes almost nothing. The task's texts are mapped into the A and B slots, one output layer is attached to the relevant hidden vectors, and everything trains end to end ([[fig-4]]).

### What it costs, and what shows it

Predicting only 15% of positions gives fewer gradient signals per step, so pre-training converges more slowly than a left-to-right run ([[mlm-convergence-cost]]). The [MASK] symbol also appears constantly in pre-training and never afterwards — a mismatch the paper patches rather than removes.

The headline evidence is the [[eleven-task-evaluation|eleven-task sweep]], where [[table-1]] puts BERT_BASE above the size-matched GPT in every GLUE column. The causal claim about bidirectionality rests on narrower ground: [[table-5]] varies the objectives at BASE size only, over four tasks, one run per row.

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

pages.body:
Section 3 opens by organising BERT around a claim about workflow rather than about architecture: there are two steps, and only two. Pre-training runs on [[unlabeled-text]] and produces one set of weights; fine-tuning starts from those weights and adapts them to a labeled task. The paper puts this first because everything else in the section — the input format, the two objectives, the per-task output layers — is a detail of one step or the other.

### The two stages, in numbers

The same network runs in both stages: the [[bert-model-architecture|multi-layer bidirectional Transformer encoder]], at 110M parameters for BERT_BASE or 340M for BERT_LARGE (see [[bert-base-and-bert-large]]). It reads the same [[input-representation|single token sequence format]] in both.

Pre-training is where nearly all the compute goes. Batches hold 256 sequences of up to 512 tokens, so a step sees about 128,000 tokens. One million steps is therefore roughly $1.28\times10^{11}$ tokens, or about 40 passes over the 3.3-billion-word corpus. That took four days: 16 TPU chips for BERT_BASE, 64 for BERT_LARGE. The full recipe — corpus, optimizer, the length schedule — is in [[pre-training-procedure]], and the two objectives it trains are [[masked-language-model|masked LM]] and [[next-sentence-prediction|next sentence prediction]].

Fine-tuning is the cheap half. Every result in the paper is reproducible in at most an hour on a single Cloud TPU from the released checkpoint. Set against roughly four hundred TPU-hours of pre-training, that is the whole economic argument for the split. [[fine-tuning-bert]] covers what actually changes: task text mapped onto the A and B slots, [[task-specific-output-layer|one new output layer]], and gradients through everything.

### What it buys, and what it pays

The payoff the paper names is [[unified-architecture-across-tasks|minimal difference between the pre-trained and downstream architectures]]. Paired-text tasks would normally need cross-attention machinery bolted between two encoders; the paper argues that concatenating the pair and running self-attention over it already does that job ([[self-attention-unifies-cross-attention]]).

The bill comes as [[separate-fine-tuned-models-per-task|one full model per task]]. Nothing is shared at serving time — eleven tasks means eleven copies of 340M weights, since fine-tuning moves every parameter rather than a small adapter.

The evidence offered for the framing itself is [[fig-1]], and it is worth being exact about what that figure shows. It is a diagram, not a measurement: it asserts that the encoder block is identical on both sides and that only the output head changes. Nothing in it tests whether the two-stage split is the right one. That case rests on the downstream numbers in [[eleven-task-evaluation|the eleven-task sweep]], and on [[table-7]], where fine-tuning is compared against freezing the same encoder.

BERT's architecture is a stack of [[transformer-encoder|Transformer encoder]] blocks, taken as it stands from Vaswani et al. (2017) and the tensor2tensor release. It is in the paper because the argument needs a backbone nobody has to argue about: if the network is one people already train, then whatever BERT gains has to come from how it is trained rather than from what it is.

The paper is open about the omission. It declines to describe the encoder at all, pointing readers to the original paper and to the Annotated Transformer guide, on the grounds that Transformers have become common.

### What is actually specified

What the paper does pin down is size. [[model-size-notation|Three numbers]] fix a configuration: $L$ blocks in the stack, [[hidden-size-h|hidden size]] $H$ for the vectors handed from block to block, and $A$ [[self-attention|self-attention]] heads inside each block. A fourth sits in a footnote rather than the text: the inner width of every block's feed-forward network is [[feed-forward-filter-size|four times the hidden size]].

Walk one configuration through. BERT_BASE is $L=12$, $H=768$, $A=12$. Each block splits its 768-dimensional vectors across 12 heads, so one head works in $768/12 = 64$ dimensions. The feed-forward network in that block widens 768 to 3072 and projects back down.

BERT_LARGE is $L=24$, $H=1024$, $A=16$. Head width is again $1024/16 = 64$; what grows is the depth of the stack, the number of heads, and the width between blocks. [[bert-base-and-bert-large|The two configurations]] come to 110M and 340M parameters.

### The one change

The single architectural point the paper calls out is the attention mask. Every token attends to every other token, left and right, at every layer — [[bidirectional-self-attention|bidirectional self-attention]] — where the [[openai-gpt|GPT]] Transformer uses a [[constrained-self-attention|left-context-only mask]]. Mechanically this is a mask that is not applied, not a different operation.

It is not free. A stack in which every position already sees the token it would have to predict cannot be trained as an ordinary language model at all, which is what forces the [[masked-language-model|masked LM]] objective and its costs. Sizing carries the other constraint: BERT_BASE was [[gpt-size-match|matched to GPT's size]] on purpose, so the later comparison turns on the mask rather than on capacity.

### How strong the evidence is

Two figures carry this concept, and both are diagrams. [[fig-1]] shows the same encoder in the pre-training and fine-tuning panels, with the pre-trained weights carried across by dotted arrows. [[fig-3]] draws the BERT/GPT/ELMo contrast as arrow directions.

Neither figure measures anything. They state the claim clearly, but the case that bidirectionality is what pays comes from the ablation in [[table-5]], not from these pictures.

Deep bidirectionality is the property [[bert]] is named for: at every layer of the stack, the vector sitting at position $i$ is a function of the whole sequence, the tokens to the left of $i$ and the tokens to the right of it together. It appears in the first sentence of the abstract and again in the conclusion as the paper's stated major contribution, because it is the one thing the [[unidirectionality-constraint|unidirectionality criticism]] is aimed at fixing.

### Where the two directions meet

The operation itself is plain [[bidirectional-self-attention|self-attention with nothing masked out]]. Each layer scores every ordered pair of positions in the sequence and rebuilds position $i$'s vector as a weighted sum over all positions. [[openai-gpt|OpenAI GPT]] runs exactly this operation with half the score matrix set to $-\infty$, so $i$ may only draw on positions $j \le i$; that is [[constrained-self-attention|constrained self-attention]]. BERT removes the mask, and nothing else about the block changes.

"Deep" is a claim about *where* the two directions meet, not whether they meet at all. Take [[bert-base-and-bert-large|BERT_BASE]], with $L=12$ layers and $H=768$. After layer 1, token $i$'s 768-dimensional vector already mixes both sides. After layer 2 it mixes vectors that each already mixed both sides, and so on for twelve rounds.

[[elmo|ELMo]] gets two directions a different way. It trains a left-to-right and a [[right-to-left-language-model|right-to-left language model]] separately and joins their per-token outputs at the top only, so inside the left-to-right stack no layer ever saw a token to its right. The paper calls this [[shallow-concatenation|shallow concatenation]] and gives [[ltr-rtl-concatenation-alternative|three reasons against it]]. [[fig-3]] draws the whole disagreement as arrow patterns.

### The cost, and how strong the evidence is

You cannot train this with a language model objective. With attention open both ways and more than one layer, the target token reaches its own prediction through its neighbours — the [[see-itself-problem|"see itself" problem]]. Bidirectionality is therefore only trainable through the [[masked-language-model|masked LM]], which predicts 15% of positions instead of all of them.

The measurement is [[table-5]]. [[no-nsp-ablation|No NSP]] and [[ltr-no-nsp-ablation|LTR & No NSP]] share data, hyperparameters and fine-tuning; only the direction of context differs. [[squad-v1-1|SQuAD]] F1 falls from 87.9 to 77.8 and [[mrpc|MRPC]] from 86.5 to 77.5, but [[mnli|MNLI]] falls only from 83.9 to 82.1.

So the ten-point gap is mostly one token-level task where right-side context is obviously needed. [[bilstm-on-top-of-ltr|Bolting a BiLSTM on top]] recovers SQuAD to 84.9, short of 88.5. These are BERT_BASE-scale dev numbers against the authors' own left-to-right stand-in, not against GPT itself.

pages.body:
Section 5.1 pre-trains two deliberately cut-down models and compares them against [[bert-base-and-bert-large|BERT_BASE]] on five tasks. The point of the exercise is to charge BERT's gains to named parts of the recipe rather than to the package as a whole, and in particular to defend the claim that [[deep-bidirectionality|deep bidirectionality]] is what matters.

The comparison only works because everything else is pinned. Both variants use the same corpus, the same [[pre-training-procedure|pre-training procedure]], the same fine-tuning scheme and the same hyperparameters as BERT_BASE. The only thing that varies is the pre-training objective, so a gap in a column can be read as the price of one removed piece.

### Three rows, two steps

The first step deletes the sentence-pair loss. [[no-nsp-ablation|No NSP]] keeps the [[masked-language-model|masked LM]] and drops [[next-sentence-prediction|NSP]], so subtracting it from BERT_BASE gives NSP's contribution.

The second step changes the direction of context. [[ltr-no-nsp-ablation|LTR & No NSP]] replaces the masked objective with a plain left-to-right LM and keeps NSP off, so comparing it against No NSP leaves bidirectionality as the only difference.

One detail matters for reading that second step. The left-only constraint is kept at fine-tuning as well as in pre-training. Removing it would let the fine-tuned model attend rightwards after never having done so before, and the paper reports that this [[pretrain-finetune-mismatch|mismatch]] degraded results. So the LTR row measures a left-only system end to end.

### How strong the evidence is

NSP's step is small on most columns of [[table-5]]. [[qnli|QNLI]] falls 88.4 to 84.9, which is the one large move. [[mnli|MNLI]] goes 84.4 to 83.9, and [[squad-v1-1|SQuAD]] F1 goes 88.5 to 87.9. The paper describes this as hurting performance significantly; three of the five columns move by less than a point, so the wording runs ahead of the numbers.

Bidirectionality's step is larger, and uneven. SQuAD F1 drops 87.9 to 77.8 and [[mrpc|MRPC]] drops 86.5 to 77.5, while MNLI moves only 83.9 to 82.1. The ten-point SQuAD gap carries most of the argument, and it is the case where a left-only model is expected to suffer, since a token's hidden state has no right-side context with which to place a span end.

The paper takes that objection seriously enough to attempt a repair, [[bilstm-on-top-of-ltr|a BiLSTM bolted on top]], which recovers part of SQuAD and costs GLUE.

Appendix A.4 then leans on this section, using it to argue that the four uncontrolled BERT/GPT training differences are secondary to the objectives. That is an inference across experiments rather than a measurement, since none of those four differences is ablated here. The other obvious alternative, concatenating separately trained directional models, is set aside by argument and not by a run: see [[ltr-rtl-concatenation-alternative|the three stated reasons]].

sections.title: Effect of Number of Training Steps

pages.body:
Section 4 is the paper's argument by accumulation: rather than one decisive experiment, it fine-tunes the same pre-trained encoder eleven separate times and reports a new best score on each. The count is doing rhetorical work, because the claim being tested is that pre-training can stand in for a family of hand-built task architectures.

Where the eleven come from is worth walking, since the paper never itemises them. [[glue-benchmark|GLUE]] supplies eight scored tasks, [[squad-v1-1|SQuAD v1.1]] and [[squad-v2-0|SQuAD v2.0]] two more, and [[swag-dataset|SWAG]] the eleventh. [[wnli|WNLI]] is dropped and does not count. [[conll-2003-ner|CoNLL-2003 NER]] appears in the paper too, but in Section 5's ablations rather than here.

### Four shapes, one encoder

Every one of the eleven runs starts from the same checkpoint and differs in two places only: what gets packed into the input sequence, and which final hidden vectors the new layer reads. [[fig-4]] draws exactly these four shapes side by side.

For a GLUE task the [[c-vector-classification-head|head is one matrix]] $W \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times H}$ applied to [[final-hidden-vector-c|C]], the final vector at [CLS], for $K$ labels. For SQuAD it is the [[span-prediction-head|start and end vectors]] $S, E \in \mathbb{R}^{H}$. For SWAG it is [[swag-multiple-choice-head|a single scoring vector]], with the four candidate continuations run as four separate sequences.

Put numbers on that. Fine-tuning $\text{BERT}_{\text{LARGE}}$ ($H=1024$) on SQuAD adds $2 \times 1024 = 2048$ new weights on top of 340M pre-trained ones — roughly six parameters per million.

### What the sweep costs

Breadth is bought with per-task tuning. Each result is its own run, with its learning rate picked on Dev under the [[glue-fine-tuning-protocol|GLUE protocol]] of batch 32 and 3 epochs; on small datasets $\text{BERT}_{\text{LARGE}}$ was unstable enough to need [[fine-tuning-random-restarts|random restarts]], keeping the best on Dev. SQuAD 1.1 also gets [[triviaqa-augmentation|TriviaQA fine-tuning]] first.

So Dev is consulted heavily, while Test is consulted once — the [[glue-evaluation-server|hidden GLUE test labels]] allowed a single submission per model.

### How strong the evidence is

The margins are uneven, and reading them as one number flattens that. [[table-1]] reports [[absolute-improvement|absolute gains]] of +4.5 and +7.0 average points; [[table-2]] is +1.5 F1 over a leaderboard entry with no published description; [[table-3]] is +5.1 F1; [[table-4]] is +27.1 points on SWAG.

That +27.1 is the weakest of the four as evidence, since the beaten system is the dataset authors' own baseline rather than a benchmark others had competed on. The +1.3 to +1.5 on SQuAD 1.1 is the narrowest margin and the most contested field.

ELMo is the system this paper names whenever it needs a concrete instance of the [[feature-based-approach|feature-based route]] to transfer. It is also the foil the paper's architectural claim is stated against, so getting its mechanism exactly right decides how much of the claim you accept.

### What it computes

Two language models are trained, separately. One is a [[left-to-right-language-model]] over an [[lstm]] stack: it scores token $k$ from tokens $1 \dots k{-}1$. The other is a [[right-to-left-language-model]] with its own parameters and its own loss: it scores token $k$ from tokens $k{+}1 \dots N$.

Neither run ever sees the other's state. The forward stack's vector at position $k$ is computed with nothing to the right of $k$ in it, and the backward stack's vector at $k$ has nothing to the left.

The token's feature is then formed by laying the two vectors end to end. If each direction carries $h$ dimensions at a position, the joined vector is $2h$ wide. Because the two halves depend on the surrounding sentence, the same word form in two sentences gets two different vectors — these are [[contextual-representations]], as against one fixed vector per word type.

Those vectors are then frozen and fed as extra inputs to a hand-built [[task-specific-architecture]], which is where all the task learning happens. Section 2.1 reports that this advanced the state of the art on [[question-answering]], sentiment analysis and NER.

### The criticism, stated precisely

The paper does not object that ELMo is one-directional. It objects that the two directions meet once, at the very top — [[shallow-concatenation]]. [[fig-3]] draws exactly this: two one-way stacks joined only at the last step, against [[deep-bidirectionality|BERT's every-layer joint conditioning]].

Section 5.1 gives [[ltr-rtl-concatenation-alternative|three reasons]] for not building BERT that way, one of which is that a right-to-left model cannot condition an answer on a question that precedes it.

### How strong the evidence is

The head-to-head numbers are lopsided. On GLUE, [[table-1]] puts BiLSTM+ELMo+Attn at 71.0 average against [[openai-gpt|OpenAI GPT]]'s 75.1; on SWAG, [[table-4]] puts ESIM+ELMo at 59.2 against GPT's 78.0 and BERT_LARGE's 86.3.

These compare whole systems, though, not one variable — different encoders, different corpora, different task heads. The paper does not rest the bidirectionality argument on them; [[table-5]] is the controlled version, run in-house under identical data and fine-tuning.

And [[table-7]] suggests freezing is not itself the expensive part: frozen BERT features reach 96.1 Dev F1 on NER against 96.4 for fine-tuning. On the paper's own showing, the gap to ELMo is about what the representation contains, not about handing it over as features.

Fine-tuning is the second half of [[bert-framework|BERT's two-stage framework]], the step where one pre-trained checkpoint becomes a model for one labeled task. The paper's claim about it is a claim of simplicity: adapting to a task means changing what goes into the input format and what reads the output, and nothing in between.

### What actually gets swapped

The input side reuses the pre-training format untouched. [[input-representation|BERT's sequence format]] already carries two spans, A and B, so a task that arrives as a pair drops into those slots — the two sentences of a paraphrase pair, the premise and hypothesis of an entailment example, the question and passage of a QA example. A task with only one text is handled as a [[degenerate-text-pair|degenerate text-∅ pair]], with B left empty.

That a pair can be shoved into one sequence at all is its own argument. The earlier pattern encoded the two texts separately and then ran [[bidirectional-cross-attention|attention between them in both directions]]; the paper argues that [[self-attention-unifies-cross-attention|self-attention over the concatenation already contains that]].

The output side is a choice of which vectors to read. [[final-hidden-vector-c|$C$]], the top-layer vector at [CLS], feeds the new layer when the task wants one label for the whole input. The per-token vectors [[final-hidden-vector-ti|$T_i$]] feed it when the task wants an output at each position. [[fig-4]] draws four task families this way: the same encoder four times, differing only in what is packed in and where the arrows leave.

Consider how little that new layer is. For a GLUE classification task with $K$ labels, [[eq-classification-loss|the head]] is a single matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}^{K\times H}$. Three MNLI labels at $H=768$ is 2,304 new weights, against 110M pre-trained ones in BERT_BASE. That ratio is the point of [[task-specific-output-layer|adding exactly one layer]], and [[task-specific-input-output-plugging|the plugging step]] below walks it through.

### Why train all of it

Those 110M pre-trained weights are not frozen. They move on the task's labeled data alongside the new matrix, [[end-to-end-fine-tuning|end to end]]. [[fig-1]] states this as the paper's shared claim: one and the same stack in both stages, with the pre-trained weights copied across as initialization rather than extracted as features.

The paper prices the alternative once. Section 5.3 runs [[feature-based-approach-with-bert|BERT frozen]] on [[conll-2003-ner|CoNLL-2003 NER]] and gets 96.1 Dev F1 from concatenating the top four layers, against 96.4 for fine-tuning everything — 0.3 F1 apart, in [[table-7]]. The paper reads the small gap as showing both modes work, and grants the frozen route two advantages it keeps: tasks a [[transformer-encoder]] cannot express, and representations computed once and reused across many cheap experiments.

Fine-tuning is asserted to cost [[fine-tuning-cost|at most an hour on one Cloud TPU]], which is what makes the [[fine-tuning-hyperparameters|small grid]] runnable in full.

Read that evidence carefully. The two figures are diagrams; they assert the design, they do not test it. The hour has no table behind it. And the frozen-versus-fine-tuned comparison is one task, one dataset, dev numbers only — a thin base for a claim about every task.

GLUE is a set of nine ready-made classification datasets that all share one shape: read one span of text, or two, and emit a single label. BERT uses it as the sentence-level half of [[eleven-task-evaluation|the eleven-task sweep]], and eight of those datasets supply the paper's headline average.

### One head for nine tasks

Every GLUE task is fed through the same [[input-representation]]. A sentence pair fills the A and B slots; a single sentence fills A and leaves B empty.

The task-specific model is then almost nothing. Take the final hidden vector at the [[cls-token|CLS position]], written [[final-hidden-vector-c|$C \in \mathbb{R}^H$]] — 768 numbers for BERT_BASE, 1024 for BERT_LARGE. Multiply it by one new matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times H}$, where $K$ is that task's label count, and take softmax and cross-entropy: [[eq-classification-loss]].

Only $K$ changes between tasks — three for [[mnli]]'s entailment labels, two for the binary ones. For MNLI on BERT_LARGE that is $3 \times 1024$, about three thousand new weights sitting on top of 340 million pre-trained ones. The head is unpacked further in [[c-vector-classification-head]].

The training recipe is deliberately uniform: batch size 32 and three epochs for every task, with only the learning rate chosen per task from four values ([[glue-fine-tuning-protocol]]). BERT_LARGE was sometimes unstable on the smaller sets, so [[fine-tuning-random-restarts|several restarts]] were run and the best kept.

### Why GLUE, and how far the numbers carry

[[openai-gpt|OpenAI GPT]] held the previous best on many of these tasks, and BERT_BASE was [[gpt-size-match|deliberately sized to match it]]. That is what makes GLUE the paper's cleanest test: same parameter count, different pre-training.

[[table-1]] reports BERT_BASE at 79.6 average and BERT_LARGE at 82.1, against 75.1 for GPT and 74.0 for the best pre-GPT system. Subtracting gives the 4.5 and 7.0 points the abstract quotes. Both BERT rows also lead in every individual column, so the average is not being carried by one easy task.

Some care is owed to what that table is. The reported Average is not the [[glue-score|official GLUE score]]: [[wnli]] is dropped, and on the real leaderboard BERT_LARGE scores 80.5 against GPT's 72.8.

Test labels are hidden behind the [[glue-evaluation-server]], so all tuning happened on Dev — including the per-task learning rate and the choice of which restart to keep. On [[mrpc]] and [[rte]], with a few thousand training examples each, that selection has room to flatter the result.

The GPT column was read off the leaderboard and a blog post rather than rerun in-house, so the two systems differ in pre-training data as well as in attention masking. And every number here is [[single-task-vs-multi-task-fine-tuning|single-task]]; the paper mentions seeing gains on RTE from multi-task training with MNLI but reports none of them. [[table-6]] separately shows these gains growing with model size, down to datasets as small as MRPC.

pages.body:
Every input BERT reads is one flat token sequence, whether the task hands it a single text or two. The format exists so that the same pre-trained encoder can be fine-tuned on classification, tagging and [[question-answering]], with only the output layer changing.

### The sequence

Text is cut into tokens by [[wordpiece-tokenization]], drawing on a [[wordpiece-vocabulary-30k|fixed 30,000-entry vocabulary]]. The sequence then always opens with [[cls-token]]. Where a task supplies two texts, they are joined end to end by [[sentence-pair-packing]], with a [[sep-token]] between them and another closing the sequence.

"Sentence" here means [[sentence-as-arbitrary-span|any contiguous span of text]], not a linguistic sentence. A task with only one text still uses the pair shape, with an empty second half: what Section 3.2 calls a [[degenerate-text-pair|degenerate text-∅ pair]].

### The three-row sum

Each position's input vector $E$ is [[input-embedding-sum|the sum of three lookups]]. One row is the token embedding, from a table of 30,000 rows. One is a [[segment-embeddings|segment embedding]], from a table of exactly two rows, A and B. One is a [[position-embeddings|position embedding]], from a table with one row per slot up to the [[max-sequence-length-512|512-token cap]].

All three are $H$-dimensional and added elementwise, not concatenated, so the width entering layer one stays [[hidden-size-h|$H$]] — 768 for BERT$_{BASE}$. That is roughly 23M parameters of token table, 393,216 of position table, and 1,536 of segment table.

The encoder returns one vector per position. Two are named: [[final-hidden-vector-c|$C$]] at the [CLS] slot, and [[final-hidden-vector-ti|$T_i$]] at token $i$. Every downstream head reads one or the other.

### What it buys and what it fixes

The return is [[unified-architecture-across-tasks|one architecture across every task]]: a task changes what goes in the slots, not the network. Packing the pair into one sequence also means [[self-attention-unifies-cross-attention|self-attention already does the cross-attention]] that paired-text models used to build by hand.

The cost is that the format hard-codes its own limits. Two segment rows means a three-part input has no slot to sit in. The position table is learned per slot, so there is no vector at all beyond 512, and attention is [[attention-quadratic-cost|quadratic in length]] besides. The [[sequence-length-schedule|128-then-512 schedule]] leaves positions 128 through 511 trained on the final tenth of steps only. And $C$ carries nothing by itself: [[c-not-a-sentence-representation|the paper warns against reading it as a sentence embedding]], since before fine-tuning its only signal comes from [[next-sentence-prediction]].

The evidence is illustration, not measurement. [[fig-2]] draws the three-row sum, [[fig-1]] shows the same stack in both stages, and [[fig-4]] redraws four task shapes around one encoder. No ablation removes segment embeddings or swaps the packing scheme, so the format's own contribution is never isolated — what supports it is that [[eleven-task-evaluation|eleven tasks were adapted this way]] and worked.

Language model pre-training is the practice BERT starts from: train one model on a language modeling objective over [[unlabeled-text|plain running text]], then reuse those weights on a labeled task. The paper opens here because BERT is not a new task or a new architecture — it changes one component of this pipeline and inherits the rest.

The objective is what makes the scale possible. A language modeling target is read off the text itself: the word to predict is already sitting in the corpus, so no annotator has to produce it. That removes the ceiling labeled data imposes. BERT's own corpus is roughly 3.3 billion words of books and Wikipedia ([[pre-training-data]]); SQuAD, among the largest labeled sets it is tested on, holds about 100,000 question-answer pairs. Four orders of magnitude separate the two.

What comes out is not one vector per word type, as with [[pre-trained-word-embeddings|pre-trained word embeddings]], but [[contextual-representations|contextual representations]] — the vector for a token depends on the sentence around it. This is the specific form of [[transfer-learning]] the paper works in: the first task is predicting text from text, and the second is whatever [[downstream-task|labeled end task]] you have, whether it wants one label per sequence ([[sentence-level-tasks]]) or one per token ([[token-level-tasks]]).

### The part the paper is about to attack

The introduction sorts prior work by how the pre-trained model is used downstream — frozen as features, as in [[elmo|ELMo]], or fine-tuned end to end, as in [[openai-gpt|OpenAI GPT]]. That split is set out under [[transfer-strategies]].

The paper's point is that the split is the less interesting difference. Both families pre-train with the same objective: a [[left-to-right-language-model|unidirectional language model]]. Everything the argument in [[unidirectionality-constraint]] turns on follows from that shared choice.

The cost is paid once and unevenly. Pre-training is a large fixed expense — a million updates over the corpus — while adapting the result to a task takes under an hour on one Cloud TPU. You buy a general model expensively and specialize it cheaply, many times.

### How firm the evidence is

Thin, on this page specifically. The claim that pre-training helps is carried by citation — Dai and Le, ELMo, GPT, ULMFiT — not re-tested here; the paper runs no from-scratch baseline against its own tasks.

Its own contribution to the claim is about scale rather than existence. [[table-6]] shows downstream accuracy still rising with model size, and [[fig-5]] shows MNLI accuracy still climbing at a million pre-training steps. [[table-1]] shows the end result, but it measures BERT, not pre-training in general.

Masked LM is the objective BERT is pre-trained with on [[unlabeled-text]]: pick token positions at random, hide what was there, and train the model to name the original token from everything around it. It is here because the paper's central claim, [[deep-bidirectionality|every layer conditioning on both sides at once]], has no training procedure behind it otherwise.

A standard conditional language model predicts each token from the tokens before it. Let that model see both sides and the target reaches its own prediction through the layers below, which is the [[see-itself-problem]]. In the paper's phrasing, the model could then predict the target trivially. Masking breaks that path by deleting the answer from the input before the encoder ever reads it. The paper adds that this procedure already has an older name, the [[cloze-task]].

### The operation

The input is WordPiece tokens. The data generator picks [[masking-rate-15-percent|15% of the positions]] at random for prediction; on a 512-token sequence that is roughly 77 positions.

What happens to a chosen position is not simply substitution with the [MASK] placeholder ([[mask-token]]), because that symbol appears constantly in pre-training and never at fine-tuning, a [[pretrain-finetune-mismatch]]. The [[masking-recipe-80-10-10|80/10/10 recipe]] spreads the corruption across three cases. Counted over the whole sequence, 12% of tokens become [MASK], 1.5% become a random token, and 1.5% are left untouched.

The original token is the target in all three cases. Because the encoder is never told which positions are targets or which were swapped, it has to keep a contextual representation of every token, not just the visibly corrupted ones.

At each chosen position the final hidden vector $T_i \in \mathbb{R}^H$ ([[final-hidden-vector-ti]]) is fed to an [[mlm-output-softmax|output softmax]] over the 30,000-token [[wordpiece-vocabulary-30k|vocabulary]] and scored with cross-entropy. Positions that were not chosen contribute nothing to the loss, which is the [[denoising-autoencoder-contrast|difference from a denoising autoencoder]].

### What it costs, and what shows it

Only 15% of positions produce gradient per step, so each step teaches less than a left-to-right step does; see [[mlm-convergence-cost]].

The main evidence is [[table-5]]. Holding data, architecture and fine-tuning fixed, swapping MLM for a [[left-to-right-language-model]] drops SQuAD from 88.5 to 77.8 F1, and bolting a BiLSTM on top recovers only part of that while making GLUE slightly worse. [[fig-5]] adds that MLM starts behind on MNLI and passes the left-to-right model well before 100k steps.

Both are single runs at BASE size, on dev sets, with no variance reported, so read them as one clean comparison rather than a measured effect size. The 15% rate is stated, never varied. Only the mixture is ablated, in [[table-8]], and there the fine-tuned scores barely move; the recipe is defended by one frozen-feature NER column worth 0.9 F1.

pages.body:
Next sentence prediction is the second of BERT's two pre-training objectives, running alongside the [[masked-language-model|masked LM]] on the same batches. The paper's stated reason for adding it is that tasks like [[question-answering|question answering]] and [[natural-language-inference|natural language inference]] turn on the relationship between two pieces of text, and a language model, which only ever predicts a token from its context, is never asked to represent that relationship directly.

### The operation

Every pre-training example is already two spans rather than one, because [[sentence-pair-packing|a span A and a span B are packed into a single sequence]]. NSP asks one yes/no question about that pair: did B actually follow A in the corpus?

The label costs nothing to obtain. When [[training-sequence-generation|the example is assembled]], half the time B is the text that genuinely came next in the document, and half the time B is a span sampled at random from elsewhere in the corpus. Those are the [[isnext-notnext|IsNext and NotNext labels]], balanced 50/50 by construction.

The decision is read off one position. Every sequence begins with the [[cls-token|[CLS] token]], and its top-layer output [[final-hidden-vector-c|C]] is a single $H$-dimensional vector — $H=768$ for BERT_BASE. A classification layer projects $C$ down to two logits, and a softmax over them gives IsNext versus NotNext.

That head is the only new machinery: no labels to collect, no second forward pass, one small matrix. Its cross-entropy is simply added on, since the [[combined-pretraining-loss|training loss is the sum]] of the mean masked-LM likelihood and the mean NSP likelihood.

Two consequences the paper flags itself. Because $C$ was trained this way, [[c-not-a-sentence-representation|it should not be read as a sentence embedding]] without fine-tuning. And unlike earlier sentence-representation objectives, [[full-parameter-transfer-vs-sentence-embeddings|the whole network transfers downstream]], which is what the dotted arrows in [[fig-1]] carry.

### What the evidence actually shows

Section 3.1 reports the final model at 97-98% accuracy on NSP itself, against a 50% chance baseline. That number says the model learned the task it was trained on. It says nothing about downstream gain, and the paper points to its ablation instead.

That ablation is [[table-5]]. The [[no-nsp-ablation|No NSP]] run keeps the data, the hyperparameters and the fine-tuning scheme fixed, and deletes only this objective. [[qnli|QNLI]] falls from 88.4 to 84.9, [[mnli|MNLI]] from 84.4 to 83.9, [[squad-v1-1|SQuAD]] F1 from 88.5 to 87.9, SST-2 from 92.7 to 92.6.

The paper calls this hurting performance significantly. One column moves 3.5 points; three move under a point, from single runs with no variance reported. The direction of the evidence fits the claim, but the size of it supports something more modest than the wording.

pages.body:
OpenAI GPT is the prior system this paper sets [[bert|BERT]] up to be measured against. It pre-trains a Transformer as a [[left-to-right-language-model|left-to-right language model]] over [[unlabeled-text]] ([[generative-pretraining|generative pre-training]]), then continues training every one of those weights on a labeled task ([[supervised-fine-tuning]]).

That makes it the paper's example of the [[fine-tuning-approach|fine-tuning route]]: adapt by adding almost no new parameters and moving all the old ones. [[elmo|ELMo]] is the example of the other route, where the pre-trained weights stay frozen and their outputs are fed to a hand-built task model as features. Because GPT and BERT sit on the same side of that split, a gap between them cannot be blamed on the transfer strategy.

### The one architectural difference

GPT's stack is a [[decoder-only-stack|decoder-only Transformer]], and its self-attention is masked. Concretely: inside each layer, the query-key score matrix has every entry above the diagonal set to $-\infty$ before the softmax, so position $i$ ends up with exactly zero weight on every position $j > i$. This is [[constrained-self-attention]].

The mask is not decoration. The pre-training objective is to predict token $i{+}1$ from the prefix, and without the [[mask-token]] $i{+}1$ would already be visible in the vector that predicts it.

BERT drops the mask, and pays for it with a different objective. That trade is the whole argument.

### How clean the comparison is

BERT_BASE was configured $L{=}12$, $H{=}768$, $A{=}12$, 110M parameters, chosen to match GPT's size ([[gpt-size-match]]). Small settings were inherited too, including [[gelu-activation|gelu]] in place of relu. [[table-1]] then reports GPT at 75.1 GLUE average against BERT_BASE's 79.6 and BERT_LARGE's 82.1, with MNLI up 4.6 points; [[table-4]] puts GPT at 78.0 on SWAG against BERT_LARGE's 86.3. [[fig-3]] draws the claimed reason as arrows.

The paper does not leave the comparison there, and it should not. [[bert-elmo-gpt-comparison|Appendix A.4]] lists what else differs. GPT saw BooksCorpus alone, 800M words; BERT saw that plus 2,500M words of Wikipedia. Both ran 1M steps, but GPT's batch held 32,000 words and BERT's 128,000 — four times the tokens per update, so roughly four times the text in total. GPT also introduced [SEP] and [CLS] only at fine-tuning time, and used a single 5e-5 learning rate everywhere, where BERT tuned one per task on dev.

Any of those could explain part of the gap. So the head-to-head number is the headline, not the proof. The proof the paper offers is [[table-5]], where [[ltr-no-nsp-ablation|a left-to-right model trained in-house]] under BERT's own data, batch and fine-tuning still loses 88.5 to 77.8 F1 on SQuAD.

This is the recipe that turns two objectives into one training run: the corpus the text comes from, how a single training example is built, and how long the run lasts. Section 3.1 gives the ideas and Appendix A.2 gives the numbers, and the numbers are the part a reproduction needs.

### Building one example

Nothing here samples a sentence in the linguistic sense. Two spans of contiguous text are drawn from the [[pre-training-data|3.3-billion-word corpus]], and the paper notes they are usually longer than a single sentence. The first span gets the A [[segment-embeddings|segment embedding]] and the second gets B.

Half the time the second span really is what followed the first; half the time it is a random span from elsewhere. That coin flip is the entire supervision signal for [[next-sentence-prediction]].

The pair is drawn so the two spans together stay within [[max-sequence-length-512|512 tokens]]. Only then is the text run through [[wordpiece-tokenization|WordPiece]], and only after that is [[masked-language-model|masking]] applied, at a uniform 15% over token positions with no special handling for pieces of a split word. [[training-sequence-generation|The full ordering]] matters, because masking after tokenization means a mask can land on half a word.

### The run

Batches are 256 sequences. At 512 tokens each that is 128,000 tokens per step, and a million steps at that rate is roughly 128 billion tokens, or about [[training-steps-and-epochs|40 passes]] over the corpus. That epoch figure is computed at the full length; the [[sequence-length-schedule|length schedule]] runs 90% of steps at 128 tokens instead, and the paper does not say whether the batch grows to hold tokens-per-step fixed. So 40 epochs is an upper reading of what the model actually saw.

The [[pretraining-optimizer-settings|optimizer settings]], the [[gelu-activation|gelu activation]] and the [[combined-pretraining-loss|summed loss]] are stated flatly, without justification or a search over alternatives.

### What the fixity buys

Every number above stays frozen across the paper's own comparisons. [[effect-of-pre-training-tasks|The task ablation]] can charge a score drop to one removed objective only because the cut-down runs share this exact data, schedule and hyperparameters, so the recipe is the control that [[table-5]] rests on.

The direct evidence for the procedure itself is thin. [[fig-1]] shows what the run is for -- one stack pre-trained, then carried across intact -- but it is a schematic, not a measurement. Four days on [[cloud-tpu|16 Cloud TPUs]] is reported once and never varied, which is affordable precisely because [[fine-tuning-cost|fine-tuning is cheap]] afterwards.

SQuAD v1.1 is a collection of around 100,000 crowdsourced questions, each attached to a Wikipedia passage that is guaranteed to contain the answer. It appears in the [[eleven-task-evaluation|eleven-task sweep]] as the paper's token-level case: the GLUE tasks want one label for the whole input, while this one wants two positions inside it.

That difference is what SQuAD is doing here. It is [[question-answering]] in its extractive form, so the job is to mark the [[answer-span|span]] of passage tokens that answers the question. Because every question in v1.1 is answerable, the model never has to decide whether an answer exists at all. The output is a pair of indices rather than a class, and the [CLS] head used elsewhere cannot produce it.

### The head, in full

Question and passage enter as one sequence rather than two encodings, the question carrying the A segment embedding and the passage carrying B ([[packed-question-passage-sequence]]).

Fine-tuning then adds exactly two vectors ([[span-prediction-head]]): a start vector $S$ and an end vector $E$, both in $\mathbb{R}^H$ ([[start-and-end-vectors]]). With $H = 1024$ for BERT_LARGE that is 2,048 fresh weights sitting on top of 340M pre-trained ones.

Take $T_i$, the top-layer vector at passage position $i$ ([[final-hidden-vector-ti]]). Dot it with $S$, do that for every passage token, then softmax across the paragraph; the result is a distribution over where the answer starts ([[eq-span-start-probability]]). $E$ gives the end distribution the same way. Training maximises the summed log-likelihood of the correct start and the correct end.

At prediction time a candidate running from $i$ to $j$ scores $S \cdot T_i + E \cdot T_j$, and the highest-scoring span with $j \geq i$ wins ([[span-score-and-decoding]]). The whole recipe is 3 epochs, learning rate 5e-5, batch size 32.

Note what is absent. The [[prior-squad-systems|published reading-comprehension systems]] this is measured against build explicit attention between question and passage; here that interaction happens inside the shared encoder, and the task layer is two dot products ([[fig-4]]).

### How strong the result is

[[table-2]] puts a single fine-tuned BERT_LARGE at 91.8 test F1 and a seven-model ensemble at 93.2, against 91.7 for the best ensemble on the board. The single model edging past that ensemble is the sharper of the two claims.

The comparison comes with conditions the paper states itself ([[squad-leaderboard-public-data-rules]]): the leaderboard entries have no current public descriptions and may train on any public data. BERT matches that by fine-tuning on TriviaQA first ([[triviaqa-augmentation]]). Dropping that step costs only 0.1-0.4 F1, so the margin does not rest on it — but the opponents remain systems whose training data is not known. Both metrics are reported, and F1 gives partial credit ([[exact-match-and-f1]]).

One more reading. In [[table-5]], swapping the [[masked-language-model|masked LM]] for a left-to-right objective drops SQuAD from 88.5 to 77.8 F1, a far larger fall than on the [[sentence-level-tasks|sentence-level tasks]]. A span's first token is often only identifiable from the words after it, which is where bidirectionality pays.

[[squad-v2-0]] removes the answerability guarantee, and asks this same head for one extra decision.

Transfer learning is the frame Section 2 puts around every system the paper reviews, and around BERT itself. Train a model once where data is plentiful, then reuse those same weights on a task where labeled data is not.

The scarcity is the motivation. [[mrpc|MRPC]], one of the benchmarks in the sweep, has 3,600 labeled training pairs. BERT's [[pre-training-data|pre-training corpus]] is about 3.3 billion words of [[unlabeled-text|unannotated text]]. No deep encoder learns from 3,600 examples what it can learn from 3.3 billion words, so it learns from the second and is then aimed at the first. Tasks in that position are what the paper calls [[low-resource-tasks]].

Concretely, transfer here is weight copying. Pre-training runs 1,000,000 updates on batches of 256 sequences of up to 512 tokens, roughly 128,000 tokens per step and about 40 passes over the corpus, which took four days on 64 TPU chips. What comes out is a set of numbers: 110M parameters for BERT_BASE, 340M for BERT_LARGE.

[[bert-framework|Fine-tuning]] initialises a [[downstream-task|downstream]] model with exactly those numbers, attaches one output layer, and trains the whole thing for two to four epochs. The paper puts that second stage at [[fine-tuning-cost|at most an hour on a single Cloud TPU]].

So the expensive half is paid once, and each of the eleven tasks pays only the cheap half. That is the trade the whole paper rests on.

Section 2 sorts the sources. Text with no labels is one, and is where [[language-model-pre-training|language model pre-training]] lives; that is the particular instance of transfer this paper works in. The other is [[supervised-transfer-learning|transfer from a large labeled task]], which gets a single paragraph citing inference and translation, plus ImageNet fine-tuning as the vision analogue. None of BERT's own results use it. How the copied weights are then attached to the target task is a separate question, answered by the paper's taxonomy in [[transfer-strategies]].

### What the evidence actually covers

The paper never trains its architecture from scratch on a downstream task. No ablation carries a randomly initialised baseline, so the claim that transfer helps at all is inherited from the work Section 2 reviews rather than measured here. What is measured is variation inside transfer.

[[table-6]] pre-trains six sizes and finds larger strictly better on four GLUE tasks, MRPC included. That is Dev accuracy averaged over five fine-tuning restarts on four tasks, and the paper offers only a [[few-random-parameters-hypothesis|hypothesis]] for why small tasks benefit. [[table-7]] shows frozen features landing 0.3 F1 behind full fine-tuning, on one dataset. [[table-1]] carries the headline gains. The conclusion's claim, that unsupervised pre-training is now an integral part of language understanding systems, is broader than any single table.

Before proposing anything, the paper sorts all prior [[language-model-pre-training|language model pre-training]] work into exactly two strategies for getting pre-trained weights onto a labeled [[downstream-task|end task]]. The split is here because BERT is defined by it: the paper places itself in one branch and makes the other branch's flagship its comparison point.

### What the two strategies actually do

Both begin from the same object — a network whose weights were trained on [[unlabeled-text]]. What differs is what happens to those weights once labeled data arrives.

In the [[feature-based-approach]], the pre-trained network is run over the input and then left alone. Its hidden vectors are read out and handed to a second model, designed by hand for the task, which is trained from scratch. Gradients stop at the frozen boundary. The pre-trained weights never move. [[elmo]] is the paper's example.

In the [[fine-tuning-approach]], one small output layer is attached and gradients flow through everything. For a 340M-parameter encoder, all 340M parameters are updated on the task's labeled data, alongside the handful of new ones ([[minimal-task-specific-parameters]]). [[openai-gpt]] is the paper's example.

Each side pays something. Freezing means you compute the expensive representation once and then run many cheap experiments on top, and it lets you attach a [[task-specific-architecture]] for tasks a [[transformer-encoder]] cannot express directly. Fine-tuning gives up both of those — you get a separate full-size model and a full training run per task — and buys the ability to reshape the representation for the task.

### Why the split carries weight

The paper's argument turns on what the two strategies share rather than what separates them: both pre-trained with a unidirectional language model. So the [[unidirectionality-constraint]] is a property of the objective, not of the transfer method.

That constraint bites harder in the fine-tuning branch. There the pre-trained architecture *is* the downstream architecture, so a left-to-right attention mask cannot be undone by an output layer. The feature-based branch can paper over it after the fact by concatenating two separately trained directions ([[fig-3]]).

### How strong the evidence is

The paper later tests the choice on itself. [[feature-based-approach-with-bert|Freezing BERT]] on [[conll-2003-ner|CoNLL-2003 NER]] and [[concat-last-four-layers|concatenating its top four layers]] lands 0.3 F1 behind fine-tuning the whole thing ([[table-7]]).

That is one task, one dataset, with hyperparameters chosen on Dev and scores averaged over five restarts. It supports the modest claim the paper makes — BERT works either way — and not much more. The separate suggestion that fine-tuning is what lets small tasks benefit from very large encoders is stated as a [[few-random-parameters-hypothesis|hypothesis]], not tested.

Every method the paper builds on pre-trains a language model, and a standard language model reads in one direction only. The paper's claim is that this is not a small implementation detail: it decides which architectures can be pre-trained at all, and for [[fine-tuning-approach|fine-tuning approaches]] the restricted architecture is also the one that gets used on the end task.

### Where the one direction actually lives

The constraint comes from the objective before it comes from the network. A [[left-to-right-language-model|left-to-right language model]] scores text as $\prod_t p(x_t \mid x_1 \ldots x_{t-1})$, so the prediction at position $t$ may see positions $1$ through $t-1$ and nothing else.

That factorisation has to be enforced inside the model, or the objective is meaningless. In a Transformer it is enforced in the attention scores: before the softmax, every score from position $t$ to a position later than $t$ is set to $-\infty$, so those attention weights come out as zero. The paper calls the result [[constrained-self-attention|constrained self-attention]], and [[openai-gpt|OpenAI GPT]] applies it in every one of its layers.

Follow one token through such a stack. Token 3 of a 20-token sentence enters layer 1 able to attend to 3 positions, and leaves layer 1 as a mixture of those 3. It enters layer 2 able to attend to the layer-1 outputs of the same 3 positions.

Twelve layers later, its vector still depends on nothing to its right. Depth re-mixes what the mask allowed through; it never restores what the mask removed.

The obvious repair — drop the mask — breaks the training signal instead, which is [[see-itself-problem|the "see itself" problem]] that [[masked-language-model|masked LM]] is introduced to get around.

### What the paper says it costs, and how well that is shown

The paper states two costs, and hedges them differently. For [[sentence-level-tasks|sentence-level tasks]] the restriction is called sub-optimal. For [[token-level-tasks|token-level tasks]] such as [[question-answering|question answering]] it says the restriction *could be* very harmful, because an [[answer-span]] needs context from both sides.

The [[feature-based-approach|feature-based approach]] softens this, since the frozen vectors are handed to a task architecture free to add two-sided machinery of its own. Fine-tuning has no such escape. That is why the paper aims its criticism there.

One workaround already existed, [[shallow-concatenation|concatenating two directional models]]; Section 5.1's reasons for rejecting it are in [[ltr-rtl-concatenation-alternative|its own section below]].

For evidence, [[fig-3]] draws the claim as arrows rather than measuring it. The measurement is [[table-5]]'s [[ltr-no-nsp-ablation|LTR & No NSP]] row, trained on the same data with the same fine-tuning scheme and hyperparameters, which the paper reports as worse on every task with large drops on MRPC and SQuAD. A randomly initialised [[bilstm-on-top-of-ltr|BiLSTM added on top]] of that model, as a good-faith attempt to supply right-side context, recovers part of the SQuAD gap and hurts the GLUE tasks.

The ablation is one architecture size, an in-house stand-in for GPT rather than GPT itself, and it arrives four sections after the claim it supports.

The paper's central claim is that pre-training should produce [[deep-bidirectionality|representations where every layer conditions on both sides at once]], and its argument is that no standard language modelling objective can be trained that way. Masking is the one move that makes such an objective trainable, and everything else on this page is what that move costs.

Start with the obstacle. In a stack of Transformer layers with unrestricted attention, a position's vector at layer $k$ is built from every position's vector at layer $k-1$. So if the token you are trying to predict is still present in the input, its own embedding flows upward through the layers into the very vector you read the prediction off. This is [[see-itself-problem|the "see itself" problem]], and the paper says a model in that situation "could trivially predict the target word." Note the form of the claim: it is reasoning about the architecture, not an experiment. No run in the paper measures how badly a naively bidirectional LM degenerates.

The fix is to delete the token from the input before the model reads it. That is the [[masked-language-model|masked LM objective]], which the paper is careful to say the literature has long called a [[cloze-task|Cloze task]]. The position stays in the sequence, and its final hidden vector feeds an [[mlm-output-softmax|output softmax over the vocabulary]] whose width is fixed by the [[wordpiece-vocabulary-30k|30,000-token WordPiece vocabulary]]. Cross-entropy is taken against the original token. The [[masking-rate-15-percent|15% rate]] is stated once and used in every experiment; the paper reports no search over it.

### The price of the placeholder

The [[mask-token]] is a symbol invented for pre-training, and it never appears in a downstream input. That asymmetry is the whole of the [[pretrain-finetune-mismatch|pre-train / fine-tune mismatch]] the paper worries about. To soften it, only 80% of chosen positions actually become [MASK]: this is the [[masking-recipe-80-10-10|80/10/10 recipe]], one particular mixture of [[mask-same-rnd-strategies|the three things that can happen to a selected token]]. The original token is the target in all three cases, so the model cannot learn that a prediction is only ever wanted where a placeholder sits.

Then the [[masking-procedure-ablation|masking ablation]] undercuts the motivation. [[table-8]] pre-trains six models that differ only in the mixture. On fine-tuned MNLI the whole spread is 83.6 to 84.4, and using [MASK] 100% of the time scores 84.3 against the recipe's 84.2 — slightly ahead. On this evidence, the recipe is not what makes fine-tuned BERT work.

It earns its keep only where the model is frozen. That is the point of [[feature-based-amplifies-mask-mismatch|the feature-based column]]: with BERT's weights fixed, and features taken from [[concat-last-four-layers|the top four layers concatenated]], a pre-training habit cannot be adapted away. There, all-[MASK] falls from 94.9 to 94.0 NER F1. That 0.9 points is the clearest effect in the table, and it is still under a point.

### The price per step

A [[left-to-right-language-model|left-to-right model]] gets a target at every position; masking 15% leaves roughly one position in seven producing gradient. [[mlm-convergence-cost|Slower convergence]] follows, and the paper confirms it, adding that MLM's absolute MNLI accuracy overtakes the left-to-right model's "almost immediately". [[fig-5]] shows the qualifier matters: at the earliest plotted checkpoint the left-to-right model is ahead. The same figure supports [[training-steps-and-epochs|the full million-step budget]] with about 1.0 point of MNLI between 500k and 1M steps, though the curve moves only a few tenths over the last stretch.

So the chain holds at its ends and is thinner in the middle. That the objective swap helps downstream is measured. That masking is the only available fix, that 15% is the right rate, and that the mixture matters — those are argued, assumed, or, in the mixture's case, measured and found small.
