pages.body:
The paper's argument here is that once the encoder has been pre-trained bidirectionally, adapting it to a task needs almost no new machinery — [[task-specific-output-layer|a single added output layer]], and sometimes just a vector. The evidence offered is four tasks whose heads shrink to that size and still outscore the hand-built architectures they replace.

The design goal has a name in the paper: [[minimal-task-specific-parameters|as few new weights as possible]]. What follows is the paper walking that goal across four task shapes without ever growing the head.

### Counting what each head adds

For a GLUE classification task the head is one weight matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times H}$ applied to [[final-hidden-vector-c|C]], the top-layer vector at the [[cls-token|[CLS]]] position, then a softmax and a cross-entropy loss. That expression, [[eq-classification-loss|$\log(\mathrm{softmax}(CW^T))$]], is the whole [[c-vector-classification-head|task-specific model]].

Put numbers on it. MNLI has three labels and BERT_LARGE has $H = 1024$, so $W$ holds $3 \times 1024 = 3{,}072$ weights, against 340 million pre-trained ones. That is roughly one new parameter for every hundred thousand carried over.

Extractive [[question-answering]] needs per-token output rather than one pooled vector, so the head reads [[final-hidden-vector-ti|$T_i$]] instead of $C$. The paper adds [[start-and-end-vectors|a start vector $S$ and an end vector $E$]], each of dimension $H$. [[eq-span-start-probability|The start distribution]] is a softmax of $S \cdot T_i$ over the passage; the end distribution is the same formula with $E$. That is 2,048 new numbers, and [[span-prediction-head|the entire span head]].

[[eq-span-score|A candidate span]] from $i$ to $j$ scores $S \cdot T_i + E \cdot T_j$, and [[span-score-and-decoding|the best pair with $j \geq i$ wins]]. This is where the contrast lands: [[prior-squad-systems|the published systems in Table 2]] built attention machinery between question and passage by hand, and on [[squad-v1-1|SQuAD v1.1]] a single fine-tuned BERT_LARGE reaches 91.8 test F1 against 88.5 for the best published ensemble ([[table-2]]).

[[squad-v2-0|SQuAD v2.0]] drops the guarantee that the passage contains [[answer-span|an answer span]] at all. Rather than add an answerability classifier, the paper scores abstention as [[cls-as-null-span|a span starting and ending at [CLS]]]: [[null-span-score|$s_{null} = S \cdot C + E \cdot C$]], reusing $S$ and $E$ unchanged. Zero new parameters, and 83.1 test F1 against 78.0 for the best prior system ([[table-3]]).

[[swag-multiple-choice-head|SWAG]] packs each of four continuations into its own sequence and dots one learned vector with each sequence's $C$ ([[fig-4]]) — 86.3% test accuracy, +27.1 points over the dataset authors' baseline ([[table-4]]).

### What this does not establish

The paper never runs the ablation the argument would want. No experiment holds the encoder fixed and compares a small head against a large one, so "the small head suffices" is inferred from winning, not isolated by measurement. Each comparison changes the head, the encoder and the pre-training together.

Two smaller caveats. [[tau-threshold|The threshold τ]] in [[eq-null-answer-threshold|the answering rule]] is fitted on dev to maximise F1 — the same metric reported on test — and the paper gives neither its value nor a sensitivity curve. The SQuAD 1.1 numbers also include TriviaQA fine-tuning first, worth 0.1–0.4 F1 by the paper's own account, which is a data change rather than a head change.

Section 5.2 offers a reason the design might help on small datasets: with few randomly initialised parameters, task models can exploit a larger pre-trained representation. The paper states that as a hypothesis and does not test it.

One property of the decoding rule is worth reading plainly. The span score is additive, so start and end are picked jointly at decoding time but their distributions were trained independently, and nothing in the score checks that the result is a well-formed phrase. Note also that [[exact-match-and-f1|EM and F1]] disagree by several points on every row — 85.1 EM against 91.8 F1 — so which metric is quoted changes how wide the margin looks.

The argument this page traces is that BERT does not reshape its network for each task — it reshapes each task into one input format, and the network stays put. The claim of a [[unified-architecture-across-tasks|unified architecture]] therefore rests almost entirely on the input representation, not on anything the encoder does.

Start with what the paper declines to invent. [[bert-model-architecture|BERT's architecture]] is a [[transformer-encoder|Transformer encoder]], and the paper says its implementation is almost identical to the original, so it omits the description and points readers at Vaswani et al. and at the "Annotated Transformer" guide.

What it does give are three dials: [[model-size-notation|L layers, hidden size H, and A attention heads]]. [[bert-base-and-bert-large|BERT_BASE]] sets them to 12, 768 and 12, for 110M parameters; BERT_LARGE to 24, 1024 and 16, for 340M.

One thing about the encoder is changed. [[self-attention|Self-attention]] normally lets each position mix information from the positions it is permitted to see, and the permission is set by a mask. BERT removes the mask, so every token attends left and right at every layer — [[bidirectional-self-attention|bidirectional self-attention]], against the [[constrained-self-attention|left-only masking]] GPT uses. The paper says this masking is the only architectural difference between BERT_BASE and GPT.

### The format carries the load

The [[input-representation|input/output representation]] is a single token sequence that can hold either one span of text or two. Text is split by [[wordpiece-tokenization|WordPiece]] into a [[wordpiece-vocabulary-30k|30,000-token vocabulary]], and each token's input vector is the [[input-embedding-sum|elementwise sum of three learned rows]]: what the token is, which span it sits in, and where it sits. [[fig-2]] draws the three rows joined by plus signs rather than concatenated, so the input width stays $H$ no matter how many signals are added.

Every sequence opens with [CLS], whose top-layer vector [[final-hidden-vector-c|$C \in \mathbb{R}^H$]] is read as the aggregate; it is just the [[final-hidden-vector-ti|$T_i$]] at position zero, given its own name.

From there each task family is a packing exercise. Two texts become [[sentence-pair-packing|span A and span B]] in one sequence, told apart by [SEP] and by [[segment-embeddings|a learned A/B embedding]] on every token. SQuAD reuses that directly as a [[packed-question-passage-sequence|question tagged A and passage tagged B]]. A single text becomes a [[degenerate-text-pair|pair whose B half is empty]]. Tagging needs one extra rule, because WordPiece may split a labelled word: [[first-sub-token-classification|the first piece's vector carries the tag]].

The consequence is that adaptation happens in the slots, not the stack. [[fig-1]] draws pre-training and fine-tuning as the same encoder twice, and [[fig-4]] draws four task families as four copies of one diagram. What is left over is [[minimal-task-specific-parameters|a very small set of new weights]] — one matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times H}$ for GLUE, two vectors $S$ and $E$ for SQuAD — against the [[task-specific-architecture|hand-built per-task model]] the feature-based route assumes.

### Where the evidence stops

The measured part is the accuracy: +4.5 and +7.0 GLUE average points for the two sizes, 80.5 against GPT's 72.8 on the leaderboard, +1.3 F1 over the top SQuAD system as a single model. Those show the shared setup wins; they do not isolate the format as the reason.

The [[self-attention-unifies-cross-attention|claim that self-attention over a concatenated pair already includes]] [[bidirectional-cross-attention|cross attention between the two texts]] is stated, not tested. No ablation encodes the pair separately and compares under otherwise identical conditions. Read strictly, it is an argument about what unmasked attention can express, which is my reading rather than the paper's wording.

Figure 4 is an illustration, so it demonstrates the claim's shape and leaves accuracy to the tables.

Two honest qualifications are the paper's own. Uniformity is of shape only: eleven tasks still produce [[separate-fine-tuned-models-per-task|eleven fine-tuned models]] from one checkpoint. And Section 5.3 concedes that not all tasks are easily represented by a Transformer encoder, so some still need an architecture added.

The headline tables argue by winning; this part of the paper argues by subtraction. Train a model with one piece removed, hold everything else fixed, and charge whatever the score loses to that piece.

The control makes the arithmetic mean something. [[effect-of-pre-training-tasks|The two cut-down runs]] use the same corpus, the same fine-tuning scheme and the same hyperparameters as BERT_BASE — the whole [[pre-training-procedure|recipe]] except the one deleted part. Without that, a drop could be charged to data or to a learning rate instead.

### Bidirectionality is where the weight falls

[[no-nsp-ablation|No NSP]] keeps masked prediction and deletes the sentence-pair task. [[ltr-no-nsp-ablation|LTR & No NSP]] goes one step further and swaps masked prediction for an ordinary [[left-to-right-language-model|left-to-right language model]]. In the network that means [[constrained-self-attention|masking attention]] so each position may attend only to positions on its left.

Comparing those two runs charges the gap to the direction of context alone. In [[table-5]] SQuAD F1 falls from 87.9 to 77.8, and MRPC from 86.5 to 77.5. MNLI moves much less, 83.9 to 82.1.

So the case for [[deep-bidirectionality]] is carried mainly by the token-level task, where right-side context is plainly needed to decide where an [[answer-span]] ends. The sentence-level evidence for it is real but thin.

One procedural detail shapes that number. The left-only constraint was applied at fine-tuning too, because lifting it opened a [[pretrain-finetune-mismatch|gap between pre-training and fine-tuning conditions]] that the authors say degraded scores. That is reported, not measured here.

The authors then try to give the crippled model its missing side back, by [[bilstm-on-top-of-ltr|bolting a randomly initialised BiLSTM on top]]. SQuAD recovers 7.1 points, from 77.8 to 84.9. It still sits 3.6 below the 88.5 of the bidirectionally pre-trained model, and MRPC drops further, to 75.7. The paper reads this as showing that right context supplied late is no substitute for pre-training with it — a reading that rests on one architecture tried once.

[[next-sentence-prediction|NSP]] does worse under the same treatment. QNLI falls 88.4 to 84.9, the largest single move. The rest barely stir: MNLI 84.4 to 83.9, SQuAD 88.5 to 87.9, SST-2 92.7 to 92.6. The paper calls this hurting performance significantly; on three of five columns the change is under a point, so the wording outruns the numbers. That last judgement is my reading, not the paper's.

### Size keeps paying, for a reason that is not tested

[[effect-of-model-size|Six separately pre-trained models]] run from 3 layers to 24. In [[table-6]] held-out [[masked-language-model|masked-LM]] perplexity falls at every step, 5.84 down to 3.23, and fine-tuned accuracy climbs with it: MNLI 77.9 to 86.6, SST-2 88.4 to 93.7, MRPC 79.8 to 87.8. MRPC is the point, because it has only 3,600 training examples and still improves at every size.

That runs against [[prior-scaling-evidence|earlier feature-based results]], where more layers or a wider [[hidden-size-h|hidden size]] bought little. The paper's [[few-random-parameters-hypothesis|proposed explanation]] is that [[minimal-task-specific-parameters|fine-tuning adds so few randomly initialised weights]] that a small task can still draw on a large representation. It is offered as a hypothesis and should be read as one: no size ladder was run in the frozen setting, so the contrast is measured and the reason for it is not.

### Freezing costs less than you would expect

[[feature-based-approach-with-bert|Frozen BERT]] on [[conll-2003-ner]] reaches 96.1 Dev F1 with [[concat-last-four-layers|the top four layers concatenated]], against 96.4 for [[fine-tuning-bert|full fine-tuning]] in [[table-7]]. The top layer alone scores 94.9, below the second-to-last at 95.6, which suggests it has specialised toward the pre-training objectives. The frozen rows report Dev only, so the 0.3 gap is never checked on test.

The saving is not free. Freezing puts a [[task-specific-architecture|hand-built model]] back on top — here a [[frozen-feature-bilstm-classifier|two-layer 768-dimensional BiLSTM]] — where fine-tuned NER needed only [[tagging-without-crf|a per-token classifier]]. And a frozen model cannot adjust away from habits formed around [MASK], which is the paper's stated reason for expecting the [[feature-based-amplifies-mask-mismatch|masking mismatch to bite hardest here]].

The paper's case is made by breadth rather than by any single result: one pre-trained encoder, one small output layer per task, and a better number on every task it was fine-tuned on. What the [[eleven-task-evaluation|eleven-task sweep]] shows depends on how the scoreboard was assembled — which tasks were counted, which split chose the model, what extra training data was allowed — and the paper states most of them openly, so the headline averages read narrower than they first look.

### The protocol that makes the scoreboard affordable

Start with cost. [[fine-tuning-cost|Fine-tuning]] any result in the paper takes at most an hour on one Cloud TPU, starting from the pre-trained checkpoint.

That price is what permits [[exhaustive-hyperparameter-search|running the whole grid]]. The [[fine-tuning-hyperparameters|grid]] is two batch sizes, three learning rates and three epoch counts, so eighteen runs cover a task.

Selection then has to happen somewhere. GLUE does not hand out test labels; the [[glue-evaluation-server|evaluation server]] scores submitted predictions, and the paper made one submission per model size. So Dev decides everything, which is why the [[glue-fine-tuning-protocol|GLUE protocol]] pins batch size at 32 and epochs at 3 for every task and tunes only the learning rate per task on Dev.

One more selection sits inside that. [[fine-tuning-random-restarts|BERT_LARGE fine-tuning was sometimes unstable on small datasets]], so several restarts were run from the same checkpoint and the best kept on Dev.

### What the tables report

On [[glue-benchmark|GLUE]], [[table-1]] puts [[bert-base-and-bert-large|BERT_BASE]] at 79.6 average and BERT_LARGE at 82.1, against 75.1 for [[openai-gpt]]. Subtracting gives 4.5 and 7.0, the two figures the abstract quotes. Both rows also lead in every individual column, so the average is not being carried by one easy task. On [[mnli|MNLI]], the largest task and an instance of [[natural-language-inference|entailment]], the gain is 4.6 points.

That average covers eight of GLUE's nine tasks. [[wnli|WNLI is dropped]], because every system submitted to GLUE had scored below the 65.1 [[majority-class-baseline|majority-class floor]], and the paper says it excludes the set to be fair to GPT. The caption is explicit that the Average column therefore differs from the official [[glue-score|GLUE score]]. Worth checking which way that cuts: officially BERT_LARGE is 80.5 against GPT's 72.8, a 7.7 point gap, wider than the table's 7.0. The exclusion is not flattering BERT, but two averages are now in circulation.

For [[squad-v1-1|SQuAD 1.1]], the extractive form of [[question-answering|question answering]], the comparison is against a live leaderboard. The [[squad-leaderboard-public-data-rules|top entries there have no current public descriptions and may train on any public data]], which is the stated reason for [[triviaqa-augmentation|fine-tuning on TriviaQA first]]. [[table-2]] reports a single model at 91.8 test F1, just past the 91.7 of the best ensemble it faces; [[ensembling|seven models]] reach 93.2, so the extra six runs buy 1.4 F1.

On [[squad-v2-0|SQuAD 2.0]], abstention is folded into the same head by scoring [[cls-as-null-span|a null span anchored at the CLS position]]. [[table-3]] gives 83.1 test F1 against 78.0, the +5.1 the paper quotes, with human performance at 89.5.

On [[swag-dataset|SWAG]], [[table-4]] reports 86.3% test accuracy: +27.1 over the dataset authors' ESIM+ELMo baseline, and +8.3 over GPT.

### What the scoreboard does not settle

Four gaps are visible in the tables themselves.

Table 1 prints one number per cell and no spread, so on RTE (2.5k examples) and MRPC (3.5k) there is no way to tell how much of the margin is the best-of-restarts selection.

The TriviaQA-free numbers, which cost only 0.1 to 0.4 F1, are Dev numbers; the test comparison is never run without that augmentation.

The null-span trick has no ablation against a separate answerability classifier, so 83.1 shows it suffices, not that it is the better design.

And +27.1 is measured against a baseline the SWAG authors built as a starting point; the 8.3 point margin over GPT is the more informative half of that comparison. None of these tables says which part of the recipe earned the gain; that is left to the ablations.

pages.body:
The pre-training recipe is not a list of independent settings. Each piece constrains the next, and the chain runs backwards from BERT's second pre-training task all the way to which corpora the model is allowed to read at all.

Start at the task. [[next-sentence-prediction|Next Sentence Prediction]] asks one binary question of each training example: did span B actually follow span A in the source text, or was B sampled at random from somewhere else? The two cases are balanced 50/50.

That question only exists if two spans sit inside one input and the model can tell which is which. So NSP presupposes [[sentence-pair-packing|the A/B packing]] the input format already provides. The answer is read off [[final-hidden-vector-c|C]], the top-layer vector at the first position.

### The corpus is a consequence, not a convenience

Now look at what generating one example requires. [[training-sequence-generation|Sampling a training sequence]] draws two spans whose combined length is at most 512 tokens, and half the time the second must be the genuine continuation of the first.

Both halves of that put a demand on the data. A real next span has to exist, and the text has to run long enough to fill 512 tokens. That is what [[document-level-corpus|keeping documents intact]] means here, and the paper calls it critical rather than preferable.

Hence the two sources: [[bookscorpus|BooksCorpus]] at 800M words and [[english-wikipedia-corpus|English Wikipedia]] at 2,500M with lists, tables and headers stripped, about 3.3 billion words together. Hence also the named counter-example, [[billion-word-benchmark|the Billion Word Benchmark]], whose sentences are shuffled and so cannot supply either property.

### Length costs more than it looks

The 512-token ceiling then collides with the encoder. Every attention layer scores every pair of positions, so [[attention-quadratic-cost|cost grows with the square of the length]]. Going from 128 tokens to 512 multiplies the length by four, and therefore the attention work per sequence by roughly sixteen.

Training entirely at 512 would be slow. But [[position-embeddings|position embeddings]] are learned one vector per slot, so training entirely at 128 would leave slots 128 through 511 without a single gradient.

The [[sequence-length-schedule|128-then-512 schedule]] splits that difference: 90% of steps at length 128, the final 10% at 512 to learn the longer-range positions.

All of it lands in one run. The [[pre-training-procedure|full procedure]] is 1,000,000 steps at 256 sequences per batch, roughly 40 passes over the corpus, four days on 16 Cloud TPUs for BERT_LARGE. Against that, [[fine-tuning-cost|every downstream result costs at most an hour]] on a single Cloud TPU from the finished checkpoint. That imbalance is what makes the paper's exhaustive hyperparameter grids and its random restarts affordable at all.

### How much of this is shown

One link is measured. [[table-5]] holds data, fine-tuning scheme and hyperparameters fixed and drops NSP, and reports significant losses on QNLI, MNLI and SQuAD 1.1.

The rest are stated. The 97-98% NSP accuracy in the footnote says the finished model solves the task easily; it is not evidence that the task taught anything. No run swaps in a shuffled corpus, so "critical" is an argument from what sampling requires rather than a measurement. The length schedule is presented as a speed measure with no ablation against training at 512 throughout, and [[gelu-activation|gelu]] is chosen because [[openai-gpt|OpenAI GPT]] chose it, with no comparison against relu.

The caution that [[c-not-a-sentence-representation|C is not a sentence representation]] is likewise reasoning about how C was trained, not a probing result. Reading the whole recipe as one forced chain is my framing; the paper states these dependencies locally, one at a time.

The paper opens by sorting every prior way of reusing a pre-trained model into two boxes, and then argues that the boxes are not where the problem lives. Its complaint runs across both of them: whichever route you take, the pre-training objective read text in one direction only.

Both boxes sit inside [[language-model-pre-training]], which is the particular form of [[transfer-learning]] this paper works in. The [[feature-based-approach]] keeps the pre-trained model frozen and hands its vectors to a separately designed task model as extra inputs. The [[fine-tuning-approach]] adds almost no new weights and trains every pre-trained parameter further on the labeled task.

[[elmo]] is the paper's named example of the first route. [[openai-gpt]] is its example of the second, and [[bert]] places itself in that second box, next to GPT.

The two routes have a shared pre-history worth naming. [[pre-trained-word-embeddings]] give each word form one fixed vector, and [[contextual-representations]] give the same form different vectors in different sentences; separately, [[sentence-embeddings]] compress a whole span into one vector, whereas BERT's stated difference is [[full-parameter-transfer-vs-sentence-embeddings|carrying every weight across]] rather than a single vector.

### The axis the paper actually cares about

Here the argument turns. GPT's Transformer masks self-attention so a token sees only tokens to its left. ELMo trains a left-to-right and a [[right-to-left-language-model|right-to-left language model]] independently and concatenates their outputs — [[shallow-concatenation]], in the paper's framing.

So the two routes differ in how weights are reused, but agree on the thing the paper objects to. That lets it propose a different axis: [[deep-bidirectionality]], meaning every layer conditions on both sides at once.

[[fig-3]] makes this case with arrow patterns rather than scores. It establishes what is being claimed; it measures nothing.

The measurement is meant to come from [[table-1]]. $\mathrm{BERT_{BASE}}$ scores 79.6 on the GLUE average against GPT's 75.1, a gap of 4.5 points, and [[gpt-size-match]] means $\mathrm{BERT_{BASE}}$ was built at GPT's parameter count so the gap could not simply be capacity.

### How strong the chain is

The paper hedges this itself. [[bert-elmo-gpt-comparison]] lists what the matched size does not control: GPT saw BooksCorpus alone while BERT adds Wikipedia, GPT introduces `[SEP]` and `[CLS]` only at fine-tuning, BERT's batch is four times larger, and BERT tunes the fine-tuning learning rate per task. Matched parameters, unmatched runs.

Its answer is [[table-5]], where two objectives are trained on identical data with identical fine-tuning. Left-to-right instead of [[masked-language-model|masked LM]] drops SQuAD F1 from 87.9 to 77.8, a fall of 10.1, and MRPC from 86.5 to 77.5. MNLI moves only 83.9 to 82.1. The bidirectionality claim is carried mainly by the token-level task, where right-side context is plainly needed.

Two gaps are worth stating plainly. First, [[ltr-rtl-concatenation-alternative]] — the ELMo-style option of training both directions separately and gluing them — is answered with three arguments and no experiment. Table 5 has no such row, and that claim is about expressiveness, not a measured result.

Second, the ELMo-versus-GPT numbers the paper cites (71.0 against 75.1 on GLUE, 59.2 against 78.0 on SWAG) compare whole systems. They do not separate the transfer route from everything else those systems differ in.

One consequence lands quietly in Section 5.3. Frozen BERT features finish 0.3 F1 behind fine-tuned BERT on NER. On the paper's own evidence, then, the feature-based/fine-tuning split it opened with turns out not to be the load-bearing distinction — that reading is mine, but the number is theirs.

Pre-training leaves one set of weights that has never seen a labeled example. This theme answers what has to change to turn those weights into a model for entailment, or tagging, or span extraction — and the paper's answer is: the inputs, one output layer, and nothing else.

### Getting the task's text into the model

[[fine-tuning-bert|Fine-tuning]] is the whole adaptation procedure, and the first half of it is [[task-specific-input-output-plugging|plugging the task's texts into the input format]]. That format already has two slots, A and B, because pre-training packed two spans into every sequence. A task with two texts maps onto the slots directly: premise and hypothesis, question and passage, the two sentences of a paraphrase pair.

A task with only one text has nothing to put in B. The paper handles this by leaving the second slot empty and calling the result a [[degenerate-text-pair|degenerate text-∅ pair]]. Sentiment classification and sequence tagging both go in this way, so no task needs a variant of the input format.

That leaves a question about the pair case. The usual design for relating two texts encodes each one separately, then computes [[bidirectional-cross-attention|attention between them in both directions]] — every token of one text attending over the other. BERT does not have a separate stage for this. It concatenates the two texts and runs ordinary self-attention over the whole sequence.

[[self-attention-unifies-cross-attention|The paper's claim]] is that the concatenated encoding already includes the cross attention. A token in B attends to every token in A at every layer, and a token in A attends to every token in B, so the pattern the separate mechanism produced is there anyway. This only follows because attention here is [[bidirectional-self-attention|unmasked in both directions]]. It is stated as an argument, not measured: there is no ablation that removes the concatenation and puts cross-attention back.

### Getting an answer out, and what it costs

The output side is [[task-specific-output-layer|a single additional layer]], so the number of parameters learned from scratch stays small. Where it attaches depends on the task's shape. [[sentence-level-tasks|Sentence-level tasks]] read [[final-hidden-vector-c|C]], the final vector at the [CLS] position; [[token-level-tasks|token-level tasks]] read [[final-hidden-vector-ti|the per-token vectors]]. [[fig-4]] draws four task families as four copies of one diagram, differing only in what is packed in and which arrows come out.

Two instances make the size concrete. GLUE's [[c-vector-classification-head|classification head]] is one $K \times H$ matrix, shown in [[eq-classification-loss]]. SQuAD's [[span-prediction-head|span head]] is two $H$-dimensional vectors.

Then [[end-to-end-fine-tuning|every parameter is trained together]] on the labeled data — the pre-trained encoder as well as the new layer. [[fig-1]] makes the point that the encoder is the same network in both stages. The alternative, freezing the encoder and using it as [[feature-based-approach-with-bert|a feature extractor]], is tested separately as an ablation.

Training everything is affordable because [[fine-tuning-cost|fine-tuning is cheap]]: at most an hour on one Cloud TPU, a few hours on a GPU. That cost sets the protocol. The [[fine-tuning-hyperparameters|grid]] is two batch sizes, three Adam learning rates and three epoch counts — eighteen combinations. Eighteen hour-long runs is a day of one accelerator, so the paper simply [[exhaustive-hyperparameter-search|runs all of them and keeps the best on dev]].

The authors add one caveat. Datasets around 100k labeled examples and up were [[dataset-size-hyperparameter-sensitivity|far less sensitive to the choice]] than small ones, which is where the search actually earns its keep.

You can now open any of [[eleven-task-evaluation|the eleven tasks]] and ask only two things of it: what goes in the A and B slots, and which vectors the one new layer reads.

If the [[unidirectionality-constraint|one-direction problem]] is what BERT wants to fix, the first question is what gets built. How do you cover sentence-level and [[token-level-tasks|token-level tasks]] alike without designing a new architecture for each one? The paper's answer is to build a single network, train it once on [[unlabeled-text]], then start every task from those weights.

### One network, used twice

[[bert-framework|The framework has two steps]]. Pre-training trains the model on unlabeled data with self-supervised objectives. Fine-tuning initializes the same model with those pre-trained parameters and trains all of them on a labeled task.

[[fig-1]] draws exactly that. The same token-in, vector-out encoder appears in both panels, and the only thing that differs is the thin output layer on top.

Two facts pull in opposite directions here, and the paper states both. [[unified-architecture-across-tasks|The shape barely changes]] — it calls the minimal difference between the pre-trained architecture and the downstream architecture a distinctive feature. But that uniformity is about shape, not about weights.

The weights do change, per task. [[separate-fine-tuned-models-per-task|Each task ends up with its own fine-tuned copy]], all branching from one checkpoint. Eleven tasks means eleven models.

The shape can stay fixed only because a single input format already covers both a single span of text and a pair of spans. That format is [[input-representation]], and it is what the next theme takes up.

### What the network is

[[bert-model-architecture|The architecture]] is a multi-layer bidirectional [[transformer-encoder]]. The paper does not describe the encoder. It says the implementation is almost identical to the original Transformer and refers readers to Vaswani et al. and to the Annotated Transformer guide. So everything BERT contributes sits around a mechanism it borrows.

The part that does real work here is [[self-attention]]. Each position builds its next representation as a weighted combination of the positions it is allowed to attend to. Which positions those are is set by a mask.

[[bidirectional-self-attention|Drop the mask]] and every token attends to every other, left and right, at every layer. [[constrained-self-attention|Keep a mask over everything to a token's right]] and you have the GPT Transformer, where each token sees only its left context. That mask is what makes standard left-to-right language modeling trainable at all.

Removing it is the single architectural difference the paper names between BERT_BASE and [[openai-gpt|OpenAI GPT]]. It also costs something: attention scores every pair of positions, so it is [[attention-quadratic-cost|quadratic in sequence length]].

The paper later rebuilds that mask deliberately, as the [[ltr-no-nsp-ablation|LTR & No NSP ablation]], to measure what bidirectionality buys. And it argues that unmasked attention over a concatenated pair already [[self-attention-unifies-cross-attention|does the job of cross-attention between two texts]].

### The dials, and the two settings

[[model-size-notation|Three numbers describe a configuration]]: $L$ layers, [[hidden-size-h|hidden size $H$]], and $A$ attention heads. A fourth follows from $H$ rather than being chosen: [[feed-forward-filter-size|the feed-forward inner width is $4H$]], so 3072 when $H=768$ and 4096 when $H=1024$.

[[bert-base-and-bert-large|Two settings are reported]]. $L{=}12, H{=}768, A{=}12$ gives 110M parameters; $L{=}24, H{=}1024, A{=}16$ gives 340M.

The smaller number is not arbitrary. [[gpt-size-match|BERT_BASE was chosen to match GPT's size]], so that when [[table-1]] shows a 4.5-point average GLUE gain, capacity is not the available explanation.

That reading is only as clean as the rest of the comparison, and the paper handles the remaining differences — corpus, objective, training scale — separately rather than holding them fixed.

You can now open any member here and know where it sits. The open question is the one this theme creates: with the mask gone, what objective can still train the thing?

Most NLP tasks come with a few thousand labeled examples. Plain text comes in billions of words. This theme is about the practice BERT inherits for spending the second on the first, and about the two ways the field had settled on for doing the spending.

### Training once, reusing many times

[[transfer-learning|Transfer learning]] is the general move: train a model on one large task, then reuse its parameters as the starting point for a different and usually smaller one. That is what makes [[low-resource-tasks|tasks with too little labeled data]] trainable at all.

[[language-model-pre-training|Language model pre-training]] is the particular version this paper works in. The first task is predicting text from [[unlabeled-text|unlabeled text]]. Nobody has to annotate anything, so the corpus can be as large as you can afford to read. The second task is the [[downstream-task|downstream task]]: the labeled end task the representation gets carried over to.

The paper sorts those end tasks by the shape of their output. [[sentence-level-tasks|Sentence-level tasks]] produce one label for the whole input, as in [[natural-language-inference|natural language inference]]. [[token-level-tasks|Token-level tasks]] must produce something at every position, as in [[named-entity-recognition|named entity recognition]] and extractive [[question-answering|question answering]]. Hold on to that split. The introduction says the restrictions it is about to criticise could be "very harmful" for the token-level half specifically.

### What actually gets carried over

The oldest form is [[pre-trained-word-embeddings|pre-trained word embeddings]]: one vector per word type, learned once and fixed wherever the word appears. The same idea was pushed to coarser units as [[sentence-embeddings|sentence embeddings]].

[[contextual-representations|Contextual representations]] change the unit. The same word form now gets a different vector in each sentence, because the vector is computed from the surrounding text. [[context2vec]] does this by predicting a single word from both its left and right context with LSTMs. The paper files both the type-level and the contextual line under language model pre-training, and treats the move from the first to the second as the line its own work extends.

### Two ways to reuse, and their two representatives

[[transfer-strategies|The paper's taxonomy]] splits this prior work in two, by what happens to the pre-trained weights at task time.

The [[feature-based-approach|feature-based approach]] freezes them. Their outputs go in as extra input features to a [[task-specific-architecture|task-specific architecture]] designed by hand for that one task. [[elmo|ELMo]] is the worked example: a left-to-right and a [[right-to-left-language-model|right-to-left language model]], trained separately, their per-token outputs concatenated and handed over ([[fig-3]]).

The [[fine-tuning-approach|fine-tuning approach]] does the opposite. It adds [[minimal-task-specific-parameters|as few new weights as it can]] and trains every pre-trained parameter further on the labeled data. [[openai-gpt|OpenAI GPT]] is the example — a Transformer language model, pre-trained on unlabeled text, then fine-tuned whole.

The difference is not only bookkeeping. On the first route, a new task means designing a new model. On the second, a new task means one output layer. BERT's contribution list turns that into a claim: pre-trained representations reduce the need for heavily-engineered task-specific architectures.

The paper also treats the two representatives as rivals, with numbers. On GLUE, BiLSTM+ELMo+Attn averages 71.0 against GPT's 75.1 ([[table-1]]). On SWAG the gap is wider: ESIM+ELMo reaches 59.2 test accuracy against GPT's 78.0 ([[table-4]]).

A third option is noted and set aside: [[supervised-transfer-learning|starting from a model trained on a large labeled task]] instead of on raw text.

[[bert|BERT]] is declared a member of the fine-tuning camp, and [[fig-1]] is the picture of that: one encoder, drawn twice, with only the thin output layer differing. It is later run frozen too, as [[feature-based-approach-with-bert|a feature extractor on NER]], scoring 96.1 Dev F1 against 96.4 for fine-tuning the same model ([[table-7]]).

So the strategy is not what separates BERT from GPT. Both fine-tune. You should now be able to ask the next question the paper asks: what were both camps doing during pre-training that BERT changes?

BERT is a bundle: bidirectional pre-training, a second sentence-pair objective, a lot of layers, a long training run, an odd masking mixture. Which of those is carrying the result? [[ablation-studies|The ablation programme]] answers by removing or varying one piece at a time and re-running everything else unchanged.

### What each pre-training piece is worth

The first cut is [[effect-of-pre-training-tasks|two cut-down pre-training objectives]], both trained on the same data with the same fine-tuning scheme and hyperparameters as BERT_BASE. Holding all of that fixed is the whole point: it is what lets a score drop be charged to the removed piece rather than to a lucky configuration. The conditions being held come from the standard [[pre-training-procedure|pre-training recipe]].

[[no-nsp-ablation|No NSP]] keeps the masked LM and drops [[next-sentence-prediction]]. Removing it hurts QNLI, MNLI and SQuAD noticeably.

[[ltr-no-nsp-ablation|LTR & No NSP]] then also swaps the masked LM for an ordinary [[left-to-right-language-model|left-to-right language model]], built by masking attention so each token sees only its left side — [[constrained-self-attention|constrained self-attention]], the same restriction GPT operates under. The left-only constraint is kept at fine-tuning too, because lifting it would introduce a train/test mismatch of its own.

Two ablations are stacked here, so the comparison that isolates bidirectionality is No NSP against LTR & No NSP. The only difference between those two is whether pre-training saw both sides. The left-to-right model is worse on every task reported in [[table-5]], with MRPC falling from 86.5 to 77.5 and SQuAD F1 from 87.9 to 77.8.

The paper then tries to repair the left-to-right model on its own terms, adding [[bilstm-on-top-of-ltr|a randomly initialised BiLSTM]] above it to supply right-side context. SQuAD F1 recovers 7.1 points, to 84.9, still well short of the bidirectional models. MRPC and SST-2 get slightly worse. The two sets of numbers point opposite ways, and the paper says so.

### Size, and how long

[[effect-of-model-size|The size ladder]] runs six separately pre-trained models, 3 layers up to 24. In [[table-6]], held-out [[masked-language-model|masked-LM]] perplexity falls at every rung, 5.84 to 3.23, and accuracy rises at every rung on all four GLUE tasks.

The claim being made is about the small tasks, not the large ones. MRPC has 3,600 training examples, and it still gains. That runs against [[prior-scaling-evidence|earlier mixed results on scaling]], which found bigger pre-trained models buying little downstream. The paper notes those used frozen features, and offers [[few-random-parameters-hypothesis|a hypothesis]]: fine-tuning adds almost no fresh randomly initialised weights, so a tiny task can still exploit a large representation. It is stated as a hypothesis, not tested.

[[effect-of-number-of-training-steps|The step-count ablation]] asks whether the full million updates are needed. [[fig-5]] shows about 1.0% more MNLI accuracy at 1M steps than at 500k, and the curve still rising.

### Freezing BERT, and what that exposes

[[feature-based-approach-with-bert|Freezing BERT]] tests the other axis: [[fine-tuning-bert|updating every weight]] versus extracting fixed activations, the [[feature-based-approach|feature-based]] style. The testbed is [[conll-2003-ner|CoNLL-2003 NER]], tagged with [[tagging-without-crf|a plain per-token classifier and no CRF]] reading [[first-sub-token-classification|the first sub-token's vector]].

Frozen, that thin head is not enough, so [[frozen-feature-bilstm-classifier|a two-layer 768-dimensional BiLSTM]] goes between features and classifier — [[task-specific-architecture|task-specific architecture]] coming back in. [[layer-selection-ablation|Which layers you tap]] matters; [[concat-last-four-layers|concatenating the top four]] reaches 96.1 Dev F1 against 96.4 for fine-tuning, a gap of 0.3 in [[table-7]].

That frozen setting is what makes the last ablation readable. [[masking-procedure-ablation|Varying the masking mixture]] over [[mask-same-rnd-strategies|MASK, SAME and RND]] barely moves fine-tuned scores. But [[feature-based-amplifies-mask-mismatch|a frozen model cannot adapt to the absence of the mask symbol at test time]], and MASK-only costs 0.9 NER F1 there in [[table-8]]. That single column is the evidence for keeping [[masking-recipe-80-10-10|80/10/10]].

You can now say which number defends which design choice, and where the paper is reasoning from a single column.

The paper has claimed that one pre-trained encoder, with one small layer added on top, can be adapted to almost any task. This theme is where that claim gets tested against numbers.

[[eleven-task-evaluation|The eleven-task sweep]] fine-tunes the same checkpoint eleven separate times, once per task, and reports each result against the best published system of the day. Three benchmark families cover the eleven. What changes between them is not the encoder but the [[task-specific-output-layer|single output layer]] attached to it, as [[fig-1]] draws.

### GLUE: eight scores, one average

[[glue-benchmark|GLUE]] gathers separate sentence and sentence-pair datasets behind one submission format. Its head is the smallest of the three: the [[c-vector-classification-head|final [CLS] vector]] $C$ is multiplied by one new matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times H}$, giving one score per label, trained with ordinary cross-entropy ([[eq-classification-loss]]).

The [[glue-fine-tuning-protocol|fine-tuning protocol]] is set the way it is because of how GLUE scores. The [[glue-evaluation-server|evaluation server]] holds the test labels, and the authors made one submission per model size. Every other choice therefore has to be settled on Dev, so batch size 32 and 3 epochs are fixed across all tasks and only the learning rate varies. On small datasets BERT_LARGE fine-tuning was sometimes unstable, so [[fine-tuning-random-restarts|several restarts]] from the same checkpoint were run and the best kept on Dev.

The tasks themselves range from three-way entailment in [[mnli|MNLI]] down to [[rte|RTE]], which asks the same thing with far less training data. Between them sit [[qqp|QQP]], [[qnli|QNLI]], [[sst-2|SST-2]], [[cola|CoLA]], [[sts-b|STS-B]] and [[mrpc|MRPC]].

That is eight. The ninth, [[wnli|WNLI]], is dropped, because every system submitted to GLUE scores below its 65.1 [[majority-class-baseline|majority-class]] floor. Excluding it makes Table 1's average differ from the [[glue-score|official leaderboard number]]: 82.1 in the table, 80.5 on the leaderboard against GPT's 72.8.

[[table-1]] reports both BERT sizes ahead in every column, by 4.5 and 7.0 points on average. All of these come from [[single-task-vs-multi-task-fine-tuning|one model per task]]; multi-task fine-tuning is raised only as a possibility.

### SQuAD: two vectors, then a threshold

[[squad-v1-1|SQuAD v1.1]] asks for an [[answer-span|answer span]] inside a Wikipedia passage. Question and passage go in as [[packed-question-passage-sequence|one packed sequence]], question tagged A and passage tagged B.

The [[span-prediction-head|head]] adds nothing but [[start-and-end-vectors|a start vector $S$ and an end vector $E$]]. Each is dotted with every token's final vector and softmaxed ([[eq-span-start-probability]]). A candidate span scores $S \cdot T_i + E \cdot T_j$, and [[span-score-and-decoding|the best pair with $j \geq i$ wins]] ([[eq-span-score]]).

That is the comparison the paper wants. [[prior-squad-systems|Published SQuAD systems]] were purpose-built readers with attention machinery between question and passage; BERT adds two vectors and scores higher — 91.8 test F1 as a single model in [[table-2]], where [[exact-match-and-f1|EM]] sits several points lower at 85.1.

The result carries an asterisk the paper states itself. [[squad-leaderboard-public-data-rules|Leaderboard entries may train on any public data]], so BERT is first fine-tuned on [[triviaqa-augmentation|TriviaQA]]; dropping that costs only 0.1–0.4 F1.

[[squad-v2-0|SQuAD 2.0]] adds [[unanswerable-questions|questions with no answer]]. Rather than a new classifier, abstention is [[cls-as-null-span|a span starting and ending at [CLS]]]. Its [[null-span-score|score $s_{null} = S \cdot C + E \cdot C$]] uses the same two vectors. A real span is output only if it beats $s_{null}$ by [[tau-threshold|a margin $\tau$ fitted on Dev]] ([[eq-null-answer-threshold]]) — 83.1 F1 in [[table-3]], still about 6 below the human number.

### SWAG: four sequences, one vector

[[swag-dataset|SWAG]] tests [[grounded-commonsense-inference|which continuation of a situation is plausible]]. Each candidate is packed with the context separately, and [[swag-multiple-choice-head|one learned vector]] scores the four [CLS] vectors. [[table-4]] gives 86.3%, which the paper states as [[absolute-improvement|+27.1 points]] over the dataset baseline — above the 85.0 human figure, though that rests on 100 samples.

You can now ask what in the recipe earns these numbers, which is what [[ablation-studies|the ablations]] take apart.

If pre-training on [[unlabeled-text]] was already working, why did this paper need a different pre-training objective at all? Its answer is that the objective everyone was using lets each token see only one side of its own sentence.

### One side at a time

A language model scores a text by breaking it into per-token predictions. In the standard arrangement each token is predicted from the tokens before it, which is a [[left-to-right-language-model|left-to-right language model]].

So the training signal at position $i$ comes only from positions $1$ through $i-1$. The vector the model builds at position $i$ has never been exposed to anything to its right.

For generating text that is exactly what you want. For a representation you intend to hand to some other task, half the sentence is missing.

The paper names this the [[unidirectionality-constraint|unidirectionality constraint]], and adds a second cost: it limits which architectures can be pre-trained at all. [[openai-gpt|OpenAI GPT]] has to mask its attention so that each token attends leftward only ([[constrained-self-attention|constrained self-attention]]), because otherwise the objective would be trivial.

The paper calls this sub-optimal for [[sentence-level-tasks|sentence-level tasks]] and says it could be very harmful for token-level ones. [[question-answering]] is its example: to mark an [[answer-span]] you want the passage on both sides of it, not just the part already read.

The mirror image, a [[right-to-left-language-model|right-to-left language model]], has the same shortfall pointing the other way.

### Two models is not one bidirectional model

The obvious repair is to train one of each and stick their outputs together. That is [[shallow-concatenation|shallow concatenation]], and it is what [[elmo|ELMo]] does: each token's feature vector is the left-to-right vector joined to the right-to-left vector.

Both directions are present, but only at the join. Inside either model, every layer is still reading one way.

Section 5.1 grants that BERT could have gone this route and gives [[ltr-rtl-concatenation-alternative|three reasons it did not]]. It costs twice as much as one bidirectional model. It sits badly with question answering, since the right-to-left half cannot condition the answer on a question that precedes it. And it is, the paper asserts, strictly weaker than conditioning on both sides at every layer.

That third reason is stated as intuition, not measured — the ablations compare against a left-to-right model, not against a concatenated pair.

### The gap the rest of the paper closes

[[deep-bidirectionality|Deep bidirectional representations]] are the alternative: every layer conditions jointly on left and right, so context from the right is available while features are still being built rather than after. This is the property [[bert|BERT]] is named for, and [[fig-3]] states it purely as arrow directions across the three models.

There is a reason nobody simply did this. Under bidirectional conditioning, a token reaches its own prediction through the layers below, so the objective collapses. That is why deep bidirectionality depends on a replacement objective, the [[masked-language-model|masked LM]], which the next theme takes up.

What the paper offers as evidence is [[table-5]]: holding data, architecture and fine-tuning fixed, [[ltr-no-nsp-ablation|an in-house left-to-right model]] drops SQuAD F1 from 88.5 to 77.8, about ten points, while GLUE gaps are smaller. Bolting a BiLSTM on top recovers some SQuAD and makes GLUE slightly worse.

That ablation is the paper's own model, not GPT; [[bert-elmo-gpt-comparison|Appendix A.4]] separately lists the non-architectural differences between BERT and GPT so they are not credited to bidirectionality.

You can now ask of any pre-training scheme: at which layer does information from the right first reach a token?

BERT wants [[deep-bidirectionality|representations where every layer conditions on both directions at once]]. The ordinary language modelling objective cannot train that, so the objective is what has to change. This chapter covers the two tasks that replace it, and the run that trained them.

### Masking, and what it costs

Start with why the ordinary objective fails. If a token may attend in both directions and is also the thing being predicted, it reaches its own prediction through the layers below. The paper calls this indirectly seeing itself, the [[see-itself-problem]]. Prediction becomes trivial, and nothing is learned.

The [[masked-language-model|masked LM]] answers this by deleting the target from the input before the model reads it. With the token gone, there is no path back to it, and both sides of the sentence can be used freely. The paper adds that this procedure already has a name in the literature: it is a [[cloze-task]], from Taylor (1953).

The rate is fixed rather than tuned. A [[masking-rate-15-percent|15% masking rate]] applies to WordPiece positions, uniformly, in every experiment. Each chosen position's final vector goes through an [[mlm-output-softmax|output softmax]] over the 30,000-token vocabulary, with cross-entropy against the original token. Only those positions are scored, which is the [[denoising-autoencoder-contrast|difference from a denoising autoencoder]]: the whole input is not reconstructed.

Two costs follow, and the paper states both.

The first is the placeholder. The [[mask-token]] is a symbol invented for pre-training, and it never appears in a downstream input. That gap is the [[pretrain-finetune-mismatch]]. The [[masking-recipe-80-10-10|80/10/10 recipe]] is the response: of the chosen positions, 80% become [MASK], 10% become a random token, and 10% are left alone, with the original token as the target in all three cases. The point is that the model cannot learn that a prediction is only ever demanded where a [MASK] sits. But [[table-8]] shows fine-tuning is close to indifferent to the mixture; the only column that moves much is frozen feature-based NER. The motivation is stronger than the evidence for it.

The second is throughput of signal. A left-to-right model gets a target at every position; masking leaves roughly one position in seven producing gradient. That is [[mlm-convergence-cost]]. [[fig-5]] shows the masked LM behind at the earliest checkpoints, ahead on absolute accuracy well before 100k steps, and still climbing at a million.

### The second task, and the pairs it needs

Masked LM is a claim about tokens. [[question-answering]] and inference turn on the relation between two texts, which token prediction does not directly supply.

[[next-sentence-prediction]] adds that relation as a binary label read off [[final-hidden-vector-c|C]], the final vector at the [CLS] position. Half the time span B genuinely follows A; half the time it is a random span from elsewhere, the [[isnext-notnext]] split. It costs no annotation, and it needs the A/B slots of [[sentence-pair-packing]] to exist at all.

The paper hedges twice. A footnote says [[c-not-a-sentence-representation|C is not a usable sentence representation]] before fine-tuning. And [[table-5]] charges NSP a real but small drop, unlike the much larger cost of giving up bidirectionality. What separates it from earlier sentence objectives is [[full-parameter-transfer-vs-sentence-embeddings|transferring every parameter]], not just an embedding.

### The run behind both

Both objectives are trained together: the [[combined-pretraining-loss]] is simply their sum. The [[pre-training-procedure]] fixes the rest, and one constraint shapes it. Because [[training-sequence-generation|each example samples two spans]] up to [[max-sequence-length-512|512 combined tokens]], usually genuine neighbours, the corpus must keep documents intact — a [[document-level-corpus]], which is why [[bookscorpus]] and [[english-wikipedia-corpus]] are chosen and the [[billion-word-benchmark]] is named as what to avoid.

The rest is arithmetic and schedule: [[training-steps-and-epochs|1M steps at 128,000 tokens per batch]], roughly 40 passes over the corpus; [[pretraining-optimizer-settings|Adam with warmup then decay]]; [[gelu-activation]]; and a [[sequence-length-schedule]] that saves 512-token sequences for the final tenth, because attention is quadratic in length.

You can now say what each task buys and what it costs. The next question is how much of it survives into [[fine-tuning-bert|fine-tuning]], where [[fig-1]] claims every one of these weights carries across.

A single text, a pair of texts, and a question with the passage that answers it are three different shapes of input. This part of the paper picks one token format that carries all three, and names the two output vectors that every later section reads.

### One sequence, whatever the task

Start with a vocabulary note, because the paper's usage is not the ordinary one. Here a [[sentence-as-arbitrary-span|"sentence"]] means any span of contiguous text, not a grammatical sentence. A "sequence" means the token list actually fed to the model, holding either one such span or two. So "sentence pair" below never implies two well-formed sentences.

Text becomes tokens through [[wordpiece-tokenization|WordPiece]], a subword scheme. Frequent words stay whole; a rare word is cut into smaller pieces that are all in the vocabulary. Nothing is ever out-of-vocabulary, so no input needs an UNK escape hatch.

WordPiece leaves the vocabulary size as a free choice. BERT sets it to [[wordpiece-vocabulary-30k|30,000 tokens]]. That number is not only an input decision: it also fixes the width of the masked-language-model output softmax, one logit per vocabulary entry.

Every sequence then opens with [[cls-token]], a symbol standing for no word at all. Because self-attention lets it read every position, whatever the top layer deposits there can act as a summary of the whole input.

Two spans are packed into one sequence rather than encoded separately. The boundary is marked with [[sep-token]], one instance between the spans and one closing the sequence — this is [[sentence-pair-packing|sentence A / sentence B packing]]. A separator symbol on its own is a thin signal, so a second one is added: a [[segment-embeddings|segment embedding]], a learned vector added to every token saying whether it sits in A or in B.

Order needs its own signal too, since self-attention is permutation-invariant. BERT adds a [[position-embeddings|position embedding]], learned per slot.

Three signals, one vector. A token's input is [[input-embedding-sum|the elementwise sum]] of its token embedding, its segment embedding and its position embedding, all $H$-dimensional, written $E$. [[fig-2]] draws exactly this as three stacked rows adding down to one.

### The two outputs everything reads

The encoder returns one vector per position: [[final-hidden-vector-ti|$T_i \in \mathbb{R}^H$]], the paper's contextual representation of token $i$. [[final-hidden-vector-c|$C$]] is that same vector taken at position zero, where [CLS] sits. It gets its own letter only because so many output heads read it.

That split is what makes the format pay off. [[next-sentence-prediction|Next sentence prediction]] needs both halves of it: the A/B slots to have something to judge, and $C$ to read the judgement off. [[span-prediction-head|Span prediction]] for [[question-answering]] instead reads per-token $T_i$, scoring each passage token as a start and as an end.

Single-text tasks lose nothing, because they are handled as a [[degenerate-text-pair|text-∅ pair]] with the B half empty. So one format, and therefore [[unified-architecture-across-tasks|one architecture]], covers the whole task sweep.

Worth being plain about the evidence: the paper asserts this format and illustrates it in [[fig-4]], where four task families appear as four copies of the same diagram. It does not ablate the pieces — there is no experiment isolating what segment embeddings buy, or what a different vocabulary size would cost.

You should now be able to take any task in the paper and say three things: what goes in slot A, what goes in slot B, and which vector the new output layer attaches to. Keep those positions in mind for [[masked-language-model|the pre-training tasks]], which are defined over exactly them.
